Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset s'adresse à ceux qui ont prétendu que le Miséricordieux a pris un enfant, qu'il s'agisse des Arabes qui disaient que les anges sont les filles de Dieu, ou des juifs et des chrétiens. Le sens général est : « Vous avez prononcé là une chose monstrueuse et énorme. » Ibn Abbas, Mujahid et Qatada expliquent le mot « idd » par « énorme » ou « odieux », et al-Tabari comme al-Qurtubi notent trois lectures de ce mot, dont le sens reste voisin. Al-Zamakhshari voit dans les versets suivants, où les cieux manquent de se fendre, la terre de s'ouvrir et les montagnes de s'effondrer, une exagération destinée à mesurer la gravité de cette parole : si les créatures inanimées pouvaient comprendre, elles réagiraient ainsi par colère envers Dieu. Al-Baydawi reprend cette idée en la présentant comme une image de la violence de cette parole. Ibn Abbas et Ka'b rapportent, selon al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir, que le ciel, la terre et les montagnes ont été saisis de frayeur, tandis qu'al-Razi cite d'autres explications, dont celle selon laquelle Dieu s'abstient de punir par patience. Les lecteurs divergent sur quelques formes verbales, sans que cela modifie le sens général du rapprochement de la rupture. Plusieurs auteurs, comme Ibn Ashur, notent un passage de la troisième personne à la seconde personne, qui sert à faire le reproche de manière directe. Les commentaires affirment ensuite que Dieu est au-dessus de l'idée d'un enfant, et que tous ceux qui sont dans les cieux et sur la terre sont Ses serviteurs, venant à Lui seuls le Jour de la Résurrection.

Ce passage décrit l'énormité de la parole des mécréants qui prétendent que le Miséricordieux s'est donné un enfant. Les commentateurs expliquent que les cieux sont sur le point de se fendre, que la terre est sur le point de se crevasser et que les montagnes sont sur le point de s'écrouler en poussière, tant ce propos est monstrueux et suscite la colère divine. Tous s'accordent à dire que le terme « idd » désigne une chose abominable et énorme, comme le rapportent Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada et Muqatil, et que ce verset réfute l'attribution d'un fils à Dieu. Al-Tabari rapporte d'Ibn 'Abbas que le verset exprime la gravité de l'association, car toutes les créatures, à l'exception des deux espèces raisonnables, s'en seraient effrayées. Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi comprennent le fendillement, la fissure et la chute comme un écroulement ou une colère divine. Al-Zamakhshari y voit une figure qui souligne la monstruosité de la parole et son effet sur la religion, et Ibn 'Ashur y voit une exagération visant à terrifier. Les commentateurs divergent sur le sens de l'éclatement et de la fissure : certains y voient un effondrement provoqué par la frayeur, d'autres une chute qui écrase les auteurs de ces propos. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Alusi notent que le verbe « yakādu » peut relever de l'image ou de la métaphore. Les lectures diffèrent entre le pronom au féminin et le masculin, sans changer en profondeur le sens selon la plupart. Les exégètes concluent que Dieu ne peut avoir de fils, car tous ceux qui sont dans les cieux et sur la terre sont Ses serviteurs, qu'Il les a dénombrés, et que chacun viendra à Lui seul le jour de la résurrection.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset décrit l'énormité du propos de ceux qui prétendent que le Miséricordieux s'est donné un fils, qu'il s'agisse des Arabes qui parlaient des anges comme des filles de Dieu, des juifs qui disaient qu'Uzayr était le fils de Dieu, ou des chrétiens qui en disaient autant du Messie. Le sens est que cette parole est si monstrueuse que les cieux faillissent se fendre, que la terre se fende et que les montagnes s'écroulent. Ibn Abbas et Ka'b rapportent que toute la création fut saisie d'effroi, à l'exception des deux espèces raisonnables. D'autres, comme al-Zamakhshari, voient dans cette image une exagération destinée à souligner la gravité de la parole et les ravages qu'elle cause à la religion, sans y voir un événement réel. Tous s'accordent à nier que Dieu ait un fils, car un fils suppose une nature semblable et une origine, ce qui ne convient pas à Sa grandeur. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi soulignent que tous ceux qui sont dans les cieux et sur la terre sont Ses serviteurs, qu'Il les a dénombrés et qu'ils viendront à Lui seuls au Jour de la Résurrection. Les lectures diffèrent : Nafi et al-Kisai lisent « yakad » à la troisième personne, tandis que d'autres lisent « takad » ; certains lisent « yanfatirna » et d'autres « yatafattarna » ; Ibn Mas'ud lisait « yatassadda'na ». Quant à « idden », la lecture majoritaire avec kasra est accompagnée d'une variante avec fatha et d'une autre, « adden ». Sur l'analyse grammaticale de « an da'aw », les avis divergent : certains y voient un complément remplaçant le pronom de « minhu », d'autres un complément de but, d'autres un sujet du verbe « haddan ». Ibn Atiyya et Abu Hayyan retiennent que « da'aw » signifie « nommer » ou « attribuer ».

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset nie catégoriquement que le Miséricordieux puisse prendre un enfant : cela ne lui convient pas et n'est pas concevable à son sujet. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rappellent que l'enfant suppose la parenté de nature et le besoin, alors que Dieu en est exempt, et que toutes les créatures des cieux et de la terre sont Ses serviteurs qui viendront à Lui humblement le Jour de la Résurrection, sans aucun lien de parenté avec Lui. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi précisent que le verbe « yanbaghi » signifie « ce qui ne peut se réaliser » : il s'agit d'une impossibilité qui ne tient pas à une incapacité divine. Al-Nasafi fait remarquer que le nom « al-Rahman », répété, montre que tout ce qui existe est un bienfait ou un bénéficiaire de ce bienfait, ce qui ne saurait être l'origine de tous les bienfaits. Al-Razi et Ibn 'Ashur voient dans le verset une réponse aux polythéistes qui disaient que les anges sont les filles de Dieu, et une allusion aux chrétiens qui attribuaient un fils à Dieu.

Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que ce verset vient après la description de cette parole comme une énormité : selon Ibn 'Abbas et Ka'b, les cieux, la terre et les montagnes s'en effrayèrent, et seuls les deux peuples (hommes et djinns) ne le furent pas. Ibn Kathir y voit une glorification de Dieu. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi rapportent les variantes de lecture sur « ayti » et « wuldan » sans que cela modifie le sens. Al-Qurtubi tire du verset que l'enfant ne peut être la propriété de son père, puisque filiation et servitude s'opposent.

Al-Sha'rawi distingue l'impossibilité de la chose et l'absence de convenance : Dieu pourrait en avoir un, mais cela ne Lui convient pas.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset affirme que tous ceux qui se trouvent dans les cieux et sur la terre, anges, humains et djinns, viendront au Miséricordieux le Jour de la Résurrection en serviteurs humbles et soumis, reconnaissant leur condition de créatures. Il ne peut donc y avoir parmi eux un fils de Dieu, car filiation et servitude ne sauraient se réunir. Selon Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari, le verset répond à ceux qui attribuent un enfant à Dieu, et il fait suite à des versets décrivant l'effroi de la création devant une telle parole. Al-Tabari comprend le fait de « venir » comme une soumission et une reconnaissance, tandis qu'al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi parlent d'un recours à Dieu dans la servitude et la soumission. Al-Alusi évoque aussi la possibilité d'un sens concret, d'une venue réelle au lieu du rassemblement.

Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que le verset nie toute filiation divine, que toutes les créatures sont Ses serviteurs, et que Sa science les embrasse. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Razi et Ibn al-Jawzi précisent que chacun viendra seul ce jour-là, sans richesse ni défenseur. Al-Qurtubi rapporte que certains juristes ont tiré de ce verset que le père qui possède son fils l'affranchit, avis qu'il attribue à Ibn Rahawayh pour une question voisine concernant les esclaves femmes.

Ibn 'Atiyya relie le verset à ce qui le précède : après avoir évoqué la venue de tous en état de servitude et d'isolement, Dieu rassure les croyants en leur promettant d'accorder ce jour-là de l'affection, c'est-à-dire des signes de Sa grâce. Ibn 'Atiyya rapporte aussi que la plupart des exégètes voient dans ce « wudd » l'acceptation que Dieu place dans les cœurs de ceux qu'Il aime, selon un hadith rapporté d'Abu Hurayra.

Ce verset affirme que Dieu a dénombré et embrassé par Sa science toutes les créatures, en sorte qu'aucune ne lui échappe ni ne se dérobe à Son compte. Les commentateurs y voient une réponse à ceux qui prétendaient que le Miséricordieux a un fils, puisque toute la création Lui est soumise et comptée par Lui. Al-Tabari et al-Nasafi expliquent l'ihsa' comme la limitation et l'enveloppement par la science, et le 'add comme un renforcement et une confirmation de ce sens. Ibn Kathir précise qu'il s'agit du décompte de tous les êtres depuis leur création jusqu'au Jour de la Résurrection, tandis qu'al-Mawardi, citant Ibn Abbas et Mujahid, rapporte que le décompte porte sur les souffles, les jours et les traces des hommes. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Bayd'awi comprennent que Dieu compte les personnes, leurs souffles et leurs actes, et qu'Il domine tout ce qui est petit ou grand. Ibn 'Atiyya considère que la répétition du sens en d'autres termes sert d'insistance. Al-Jalalayn résume le verset en affirmant qu'aucun d'entre eux, ni l'ensemble de leur nombre, n'échappe à Dieu. Al-Alusi reprend ce même sens. Les commentateurs s'accordent pour y voir une consolation pour les croyants et une menace pour les mécréants. Le verset ne contient pas de règle juridique, et les exégètes ne rapportent pas de cause de révélation propre à ce passage.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset répond à ceux qui attribuaient un enfant à Dieu, comme les juifs et les chrétiens, ou les Arabes polythéistes qui disaient que les anges étaient les filles de Dieu. Dieu affirme qu'il a dénombré toute sa création et l'a comptée exactement, que rien ne lui échappe, et que chacun viendra à lui le Jour de la Résurrection seul, isolé, sans biens, sans enfants ni défenseur. Ibn 'Abbas et d'autres rappellent que tous les êtres sont ses serviteurs soumis, si bien qu'aucun d'eux ne peut être son fils.

Les avis se rejoignent sur le fond : le verset écarte toute filiation divine et tout associé, et affirme la science totale de Dieu. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi comprennent le mot « fardan » comme la solitude de celui qui n'a ni biens ni soutien. Al-Razi et al-Baydawi l'entendent plutôt comme l'isolement vis-à-vis des suiveurs et des alliés, de sorte que ni les adorés ni les adorateurs ne gardent de lien entre eux. Ibn al-Qayyim note que le singulier « âtîhi » marque la séparation de chacun, même lorsque tous viennent ensemble, et il juge cette lecture plus pertinente que la distinction fondée sur l'annexion.

Al-Zamakhshari signale que la construction « kulluhum » peut se faire au singulier ou au pluriel, et Ibn 'Ashur relève que le nom « al-Rahman » répété souligne qu'une telle filiation contredit la miséricorde divine. Al-Qurtubi tire du verset une règle juridique : le fils ne peut pas être un esclave appartenant à son père, car la filiation et la servitude sont opposées. Les autres commentaires restent surtout centrés sur le sens général du verset et sur sa place dans la sourate.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset promet à ceux qui croient et accomplissent les bonnes œuvres que le Miséricordieux leur accordera une affection dans les cœurs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi comprennent le mot wudd comme l'amour placé dans le cœur des croyants, et rapportent de Mujahid et d'Ibn Abbas que Dieu les aime et les fait aimer de Ses serviteurs. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que cet amour n'est pas obtenu par la parenté ou par les intérêts, mais qu'il est un don de Dieu, et ils citent le hadith rapporté par Abu Hurayra sur l'appel de Gabriel puis la mise en place de l'acceptation sur terre. Al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari relèvent que le sin de sayaj'alu peut indiquer une promesse faite à l'époque mecquoise ou une réalisation au jour de la Résurrection. Abu Muslim, cité par al-Razi, comprend wudd au sens de ce qui est aimé, c'est-à-dire ce que Dieu leur donnera au Paradis, mais al-Razi et la majorité préfèrent le premier sens.

Les avis divergent sur le moment de cet octroi : la plupart y voient une réalité ici-bas, tandis que d'autres le situent dans l'au-delà, lorsque les bonnes actions sont exposées et que la rancune est ôtée des poitrines, comme le dit al-Jubba'i. Quant aux causes de révélation, al-Tabari rapporte qu'il s'agirait d'Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, mais Ibn Kathir juge cela erroné puisque la sourate est mecquoise ; d'autres citent Ali ibn Abi Talib, et certains s'abstiennent de trancher. Le mot luddan désigne, selon les commentateurs, des adversaires acharnés dans la dispute, généralement identifiés aux Quraysh. Les exégètes concluent que le Coran a été rendu facile dans la langue du Prophète pour annoncer la bonne nouvelle aux pieux et avertir les obstinés, et que le verset se termine par le rappel de la destruction des générations passées.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset signifie que Dieu a rendu le Coran facile en le révélant dans la langue arabe claire du Prophète ﷺ, afin qu'il annonce la bonne nouvelle aux pieux croyants et qu'il avertisse un peuple d'adversaires obstinés. Presque tous identifient ce peuple aux Qurayshites de La Mecque. Le sens de « ludd », au pluriel de « alad », fait l'objet de plusieurs lectures : Mujahid y voit des impies, Ibn 'Abbas des injustes, al-Hasan des sourds à la vérité, Qatada des gens qui disputent sans fondement, et Abu 'Ubayda ceux qui refusent le vrai et prétendent détenir le faux. La majorité retient l'idée d'une grande âpreté dans la dispute et l'entêtement. Le Razi et al-Zamakhshari relèvent que ce terme répond à la mention des pieux, car celui qui s'obstine dans l'erreur s'éloigne le plus de la piété. Ibn 'Ashur précise que le mot « peuple » signale que cette âpreté est leur caractère propre, et que leur refus procédait d'un entêtement conscient de la vérité. Ce verset clôt la sourate et introduit le rappel des générations anéanties avant eux, dont il ne subsiste ni trace ni voix. La particule « fa » y introduit une conséquence tirée du contexte : transmettre le message, annoncer et avertir. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur la facilité du Coran à être compris et retenu en langue arabe.

Dans la conclusion de la sourate Maryam, Dieu s'adresse à son Prophète ﷺ et menace les Quraych du sort des peuples qui les ont précédés. Il a fait périr de nombreuses générations avant eux pour avoir traité leurs messagers de menteurs, de sorte qu'on ne perçoit plus aucun d'eux et qu'on n'entend plus le moindre bruit de leur part. Les commentateurs expliquent le mot rikz par un son faible, selon Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada et al-Dahhak, ou par toute perception à peine audible, selon al-Yazidi et Abu 'Ubayda, qui citent un vers de Labid. Ibn Zayd le rapproche du sens de perception. Tous s'accordent à lire l'interrogation comme une négation, destinée à effrayer les opposants et à consoler le Prophète.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi précisent que la destruction a englobé les peuples passés au point qu'il ne reste ni trace ni vestige, et que les Mecquois connaîtront un sort semblable s'ils ne se repentent pas. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Razi indiquent que l'anéantissement peut signifier la mort, ou bien un châtiment immédiat ici-bas, mais al-Razi juge plus probable la disparition par la mort. Al-Qurtubi et Ibn 'Ashur rappellent que le qarn désigne une nation ou une génération, et que kam exprime la grande quantité.

La verse fait suite à l'affirmation que Dieu a facilité le Coran dans la langue du Prophète, afin d'annoncer la bonne nouvelle aux pieux et d'avertir un peuple acharné, les ludd. Pour la majorité, il s'agit des Quraych, mais Ibn 'Abbas y voit des pervers, Hasan des sourds à la vérité et Ibn Kathir des gens déviant du droit chemin.
en: The sura opens with the disjointed letters Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad, on whose meaning the commentators differ widely. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak, read them as initials of divine names: Kaf for Kafi, Karim or Kabir, Ha for Hadi, Ya for Hakim, Rahim or Yamin, 'Ayn for 'Alim or 'Aziz, and Sad for Sadiq; al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi record these views. Others, such as Ali ibn Abi Talib and, in another report, Ibn 'Abbas, take them as an oath by God; Qatada takes them as a name of the Qur'an; some as the name of the sura; al-Kalbi as a praise God gives Himself. Several, such as al-Tabari, consider the matter one to leave to God. The narrative itself concerns God's mercy to Zakariyya, who called upon his Lord in secret, complaining of his weakening bones, his white hair and his wife's barrenness, and asked for an heir. On the meaning of inheritance, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir favour the inheritance of prophethood and knowledge, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Abu Salih include wealth; al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite the saying that prophets leave no inheritance of property. All agree that Zakariyya feared the religion would be lost after him, and that he was given the good news of Yahya, a name no one had borne before.

The commentators explain that this verse opens the story of Zakariya, peace be upon him, and that its meaning is: this is a recounting of your Lord's mercy toward His servant Zakariya, that is, what We recite to you of the Quran. For al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, the mercy here is the answering of his supplication. They report that Zakariya called upon his Lord in a low voice rather than aloud, since secrecy is further from showing off and closer to sincerity; Qatada said God knows the pure heart and hears the faint voice. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi add that he may have concealed it so as not to be blamed for asking for a child in old age, a view also given by Muqatil. In his supplication Zakariya describes his weakness and old age in vivid images: his bones have weakened, though they are the pillar of the body, and his head has lit up with white hair like fire spreading through dry wood; he reminds his Lord that he was never disappointed in his earlier prayers. The commentators agree that he feared his relatives and heirs, but differ on the nature of that fear: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say he feared they would inherit his property, while others hold that he feared the religion would be lost after him. Several, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, consider it more likely that the inheritance meant is of knowledge and prophecy, relying on the hadith that prophets leave no material inheritance. The interpretations of "the family of Jacob" vary, though most take it to mean the people of prophethood and knowledge. The different readings of "yarithuni" and "khiftu" are recorded without the commentators settling between them.

This verse says that Zakariya called upon his Lord in a secret, low voice, away from the eyes and ears of people. The commentators agree that concealing one's supplication is closer to sincerity and further from showing off. Some, such as al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, add that he hid his call so as not to be blamed for asking for a child in old age, while al-Zamakhshari notes that God hears the secret and the open alike. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that he prayed at night or in his sanctuary, and Qatada says that God knows the pure heart and hears the faint voice. The scholars differ on his age at that moment: sixty, sixty-five, seventy, seventy-five, eighty, and even ninety-nine are all mentioned. Most exegetes link the verse to the prayer that follows, in which he complains of weakened bones and white hair and recalls that he was never disappointed by his Lord in past requests. They also differ on the reason for the secrecy, and each explanation is reported without the commentators deciding between them.

This verse relates Zakariyya's prayer to his Lord, offered in a low voice, in which he describes his frailty: his bones have weakened and his head has turned white with age. He then reminds God that he has never been left disappointed in his past supplications, and so he calls on that past mercy. The commentators explain the secrecy of his prayer in several ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya emphasise sincerity and avoiding ostentation; al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi add that he feared the mockery of his people if he asked for a child at such an age; al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim see it as a mark of respect and of closeness to God, who hears even the faintest voice. Most agree that the word wahn means weakness, and al-Zamakhshari notes that the bone is singled out because it is the pillar of the body. The image of the head that is set ablaze with white hair is praised by many as an especially eloquent metaphor. Regarding the phrase al-mawali, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean relatives who would inherit, following Mujahid and Qatada, and fear that they would inherit his property. Others, such as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, take it as fear that religion would be neglected after his death. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya cite the hadith that prophets do not leave inheritance, and conclude that what is meant is the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood. Several readings differ on words such as khafat and yarithuni. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur see the phrase lam akun bi-du'a'ika rabbi shaqiyyan as a plea grounded in past favours, and some commentators recall the anecdote of a man who asks a benefactor by reminding him of his kindness.

Zakariya addresses his Lord, describing the weakening of his bones and the whitening of his head, and recalling that he had never been turned away when he prayed. He then explains that he feared his paternal relatives and clansmen would not manage the community well after him or preserve the faith, and he notes that his wife is barren. He therefore asks God to grant him, from His presence, an heir who will inherit from him and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and to make him pleasing to Him. The commentators differ on the meaning of inheritance. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Hasan take it to include inheritance of wealth together with prophethood or knowledge, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari emphasise inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, citing the Prophet's saying: 'We prophets do not leave inheritance.' Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain that the mawali are kinsmen, agnates or cousins. On recitation, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read the verbs in the jussive as answers to the prayer, while most read them in the indicative as qualifiers, and al-Tabari prefers the latter. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi give several reasons for the quiet supplication, including avoiding showing off and avoiding blame for asking for a child in old age.

Zakariya asks his Lord for an heir who will inherit from him what prophets are meant to pass on, namely knowledge and prophethood, and who will inherit from the family of Ya'qub the graces God gave them, and he asks that the child be pleasing to God and to people. The commentators explain that Zakariya feared his close kin and clients after him would not be fit to safeguard the religion and its law, so he asked for a righteous son to succeed him. On the meaning of inheritance, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Abu Salih take it to include both wealth and prophethood, whereas al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kathir, and al-Tabari in the report of Abu Salih, prefer knowledge and prophethood alone, since prophets do not bequeath property, as the hadith states. Al-Hasan also speaks of prophethood and knowledge, while al-Kalbi mentions religious rank and rule. As for Ya'qub, most exegetes identify him as Ya'qub son of Ishaq, while al-Kalbi and Muqatil identify him as Ya'qub son of Mathan. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read the verb in the jussive as an answer to the supplication, while most read it in the nominative as a qualifier of the heir, and the two readings give slightly different senses. He closes by asking that the child be pleasing, meaning righteous and accepted before his Lord.

This verse records God answering Zakariyya's prayer with the good news of a son named Yahya. The commentators note that God Himself chose the name, which is an honour to the child. The meaning of the phrase 'We have not given before him any namesake' is debated. Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya, take it to mean that no one had borne this name before; this is also Ibn Abbas's view as transmitted by Ali ibn Abi Talha. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ata understand it as 'an equal or likeness': he had no peer, since he never disobeyed God or even intended sin. Ibn Abbas, also in Ibn Abi Talha's report, says barren women never bore anyone like him. Al-Razi prefers the first sense, arguing that the second would make Yahya superior to Abraham and Moses, which everyone rejects. On the origin of the name, views differ: he was given life through faith, or he revived his mother's barren womb, or he lives by wisdom and guidance. Al-Razi adds that names of honour need not have an etymological explanation. Most commentators see the announcement as coming directly from God, while Ibn Kathir and some others see it as spoken through an angel.

This verse records Zechariah's astonishment when he was given the good news of a son: how could he have a child, when his wife is barren and he has reached such old age that his bones have dried and withered. The commentators agree that the word ʿitiyy means extreme old age, the stiffening and drying of the bones and joints. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as old age and the thinning of the bones, while Qatada and Mujahid speak of the wasting of the bones, and Ibn Zayd of losing the ability to father children. There is disagreement over the purpose of the question. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as a request for clarification of how the child would come: from this wife, restored to youth, or from another woman. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir see it as wonder at God's power or a request for information. Al-Razi rejects any doubt about God's power and explains it as an expression of joy and admiration, comparing it to the wife of Abraham. Al-Sudi reports that Satan then cast doubt into his heart, a view Al-Razi finds unconvincing. Commentators also give his age: about seventy according to Qatada, and ninety-five according to Muqatil. The divine answer is that it is easy for God, who created him before when he was nothing.

This verse from Surah Maryam describes how God gave Zechariah the good news of Yahya after he had prayed. Zechariah wondered how he could have a son when his wife was barren and he had reached great old age. The reply, which commentators attribute either to God or to the angel who brought the news, says that it is so as he said, but that the matter is easy for your Lord, who created you before when you were nothing. The commentators agree on the general meaning: God affirms His power to bring into being from nothing and to change the state of the aged man and the barren woman, and the word "easy" means easy for His power, not that any difficulty existed for Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan then report that Zechariah asked for a sign of the conception, and that the sign was that he would not speak to people for three nights while remaining physically sound. Most take this as a silence without illness or muteness, while Ibn Abbas in one report explains that the nights are consecutive. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi draw from "you were nothing" that what does not exist is not a thing, a view Ibn Ashur and others also cite, whereas the Mu'tazilites argue otherwise. The readings differ between "khalaqtuka" with the first-person ta, which is the majority reading, and "khalaqnaka" with the plural of majesty, read by Hamza and al-Kisa'i. The commentators connect the passage to Zechariah's earlier prayer and see in it proof that God answers supplications and accomplishes what He wills by His sole power.

The commentators explain that Zakariyya, after being given the good news of Yahya, asked his Lord for a sign by which he would know when the pregnancy had begun. God answered that the sign would be that he would not speak to people for three nights (three days in Al Imran), while being sound and healthy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that this was a binding of the tongue without illness, and that what was forbidden was speaking with people, while remembering and glorifying God remained permitted. He then signalled to his people to glorify God morning and evening. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi take the word awha to mean a gesture, whereas Mujahid, followed by others, understood it as writing on the ground or on a sheet, since wahy in Arabic can mean either. On the word sawiyyan, most scholars read it as describing Zakariyya, meaning healthy and whole, while Ibn Abbas and others attach it to the nights, meaning consecutive. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi regard the silence as a departure from normal custom rather than an illness. Ibn Kathir notes that the request for the sign came some time after the announcement. Al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur observe that the mention of nights here and days in Al Imran refers to the same period, since Arabic may use one for the other.

The verse describes Zakariya coming out to his people from the mihrab, his place of prayer, after God had kept him from speaking to people for three nights although he was physically sound. He signalled to them to glorify God morning and evening. The commentators broadly agree that the glorification here means prayer or remembrance at the two ends of the day, and that the inspiration (awha) was a sign or gesture, as the verse "except by signs" in Surah Al Imran indicates. Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Munabbih, al-Kalbi and al-Qurtubi take this view, as do al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir.

Other views are also recorded. Ibn Abbas and, in one report, Mujahid say he wrote to them on the ground or on a sheet. Ibn Zayd says he does not know whether it was writing or a gesture, and holds only that he commanded them to glorify God. Al-Razi judges gesture to be the reading most fitting to the verse, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi mention both possibilities.

On the nature of the impediment, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report the majority view that his tongue was restrained without illness, while al-Zamakhshari cites Ibn Abbas and Qatada on writing. As for the hours, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan cite Abu al-Aliya, who identifies them with the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. The overall sense remains one of thanksgiving shared with the community, in the context of the good news of Yahya's birth.

God commands Yahya, once he is born and has reached an age of understanding speech, to take hold of the Book, which most commentators identify as the Torah, with resolve and determination, meaning to memorise it, grasp its meaning and act upon it. He then says that He gave him judgement while still a child. The commentators differ on the word hukm: Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj take it as prophethood, al-Tabari and most exegetes as understanding of the Book and knowledge of its rulings, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima as wisdom or sound reason, and others as wisdom in general. Several reports say that children invited him to play and he replied that he was not created for play. Ibn 'Abbas holds that whoever memorises the Qur'an before puberty has been given judgement as a child. Yahya's age is also disputed, with three years given by Qatada and Muqatil and seven by a report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, without consensus.

The word hanan is understood by most as mercy, tenderness and compassion coming from God; Mujahid sees it as his Lord's kindness towards him, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd as affection, 'Ata' as reverence, and Ibn 'Abbas reportedly said he did not know its meaning. Zakat is taken by many as purity from sins, blessing or righteous deeds, while al-Kalbi reads it as an alms that God gave on behalf of his parents. All agree that he was pious, obedient, dutiful to his parents, neither arrogant nor rebellious, and that God's peace was upon him on the day of his birth, his death and his resurrection. Some reports claim he was free of sin, but scholars of hadith judge them weak or mursal, as Ibn Kathir notes.

This verse lists the qualities God gave Yahya: "tenderness from Us, and purity, and he was devout." The commentators explain that hanan means compassion, tenderness and affection. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak take it to mean mercy; Mujahid understands it as God's kindly inclination toward him, Ibn Zayd and 'Ikrima as love, and 'Ata' as honour. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said he did not know exactly what hanan means. On zakat, Ibn 'Abbas links it to obedience and sincerity, Qatada and al-Dahhak to righteous deeds, al-Kalbi to an alms that God granted on behalf of his parents, and al-Zajjaj to purification. They agree that taqwa means obeying God and avoiding sin; Qatada adds that Yahya never sinned and never inclined toward wrongdoing, a report Ibn Kathir cites while noting that several of its chains are weak. The commentators connect these qualities with the dutiful kindness toward his parents mentioned next, which they regard as one of his principal traits. Taken together, the verse describes compassion placed in his heart, purity of soul and a pious conduct.

The commentators explain that this verse describes Yahya as deeply dutiful and kind to his parents, humble toward them, and never arrogant before God or before them, nor disobedient to them. Nearly all agree that "jabbar" means one who is proud and rejects the truth. Al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud give this as the meaning, while Sufyan ibn Uyayna, quoted by al-Razi, explains it as one who gives way to anger, citing the verse "you only want to be a tyrant in the land". Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi, is also cited for the view that a jabbar is one who strikes and kills in anger. As for "'asiyy", most take it as an intensive form meaning one who disobeys much, but al-Alusi holds that it stresses the negation, meaning he never disobeyed at all.

Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report, through Qatada, that Yahya never sinned and never desired a woman, a statement attributed to the Prophet ﷺ whose chain some scholars judge weak, Ibn Kathir among them, while al-Hakim declares it sound. On the phrase "peace upon him", al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as safety from Satan, from the punishment of the grave and from the terror of the Last Day. Ibn 'Atiyya, however, prefers the ordinary greeting of peace, which he considers more honourable than mere protection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also quote Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna's remark that a person is most lonely in three situations, birth, death and resurrection, and that God singled out Yahya for peace in each of them.

The commentators explain that this verse completes the description of Yahya, peace be upon him, and that the "peace" means the security and protection God grants him at three moments: the day he is born, when he is guarded from the touch of Satan that affects all the children of Adam; the day he dies, when he is safe from the two angels of the grave and the terror of that hour; and the day he is raised alive, when he is spared the great terror and the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn 'Uyayna that these three moments are the most frightening of human existence, and that God honoured Yahya by sparing him in them. Ibn 'Atiyya, however, holds that the "peace" here is the familiar greeting rather than mere assurance, since assurance follows from the absence of disobedience, whereas a divine greeting marks a higher dignity in moments of great weakness. Several commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, relate the account of Yahya meeting 'Isa, in which 'Isa says he greeted himself, and some draw from it a preference for 'Isa, while Ibn 'Atiyya concludes that each view has its merit. Al-Razi notes a distinction for Yahya, since the verse mentions his birthday, which is not said of the other prophets. Ibn Kathir stresses the mention of his being raised "alive", which may point to his being among the martyrs who live with their Lord, a view also noted by al-Shinqiti. Ibn Kathir adds that several reports on Yahya's freedom from sin are weak, the more common view being that he never disobeyed God.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ to recount in the Book the story of Mary when she withdrew from her family to a place facing east. The commentators give several reasons for her withdrawal: Qatada describes it simply as seclusion, al-Sudi links it to her purification after menstruation, and others see it as a wish to devote herself to worship. Al-Razi notes that the verse allows all of these meanings and no clear evidence favours one over the others. All agree that the east was honoured because it is where the light rises, and Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, is said to have explained that the Christians took the east as their qibla for this reason. Regarding the screen she set up, al-Sudi understood it as walls, Ibn Abbas as a veil or the shade of the sun, and others as a cloth or a mountain. The word for Spirit is taken by most, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, to mean the angel Gabriel, while Abu Muslim and others suggest the spirit of Jesus himself. The angel appeared as a complete human man, which allowed her to converse with him, and she sought refuge in the Merciful, saying if you are pious. Abu Wa'il explains that the pious person is one who restrains himself, while Wahb ibn Munabbih reports that Taqi was the name of a notorious sinner of that time, a view Ibn Atiyya considered weak.

The commentators describe Mary withdrawing from her family to a place facing east, possibly to purify herself from menstruation, and placing a screen between herself and them. God sent His spirit, identified by the majority as Gabriel, who appeared to her as a fully formed man. Frightened, she sought refuge in the Most Merciful, asking him to fear God if he was pious, and he told her he was a messenger of her Lord sent to grant her a pure son. She wondered how she could have a child when no man had touched her and she was not unchaste; he replied that this was easy for God, and that the child would be a sign to people and a mercy from Him. All agree the spirit is Gabriel and that he took human form so that Mary could be at ease with his speech. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the Christians took the east as their prayer direction because of this place, though they do not make it a ruling. Opinions differ on why she withdrew: al-Suddi links it to menstruation, others to worship, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers worship. On the screen, Ibn 'Abbas speaks of a veil or the shade of the sun, al-Suddi and Ibn 'Atiyya of a wall, and Muqatil of a mountain. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that some understood her words "if you are pious" as a reminder of piety, while others took Taqiyy to be the name of a notorious sinner of that time. Accounts of the pregnancy's length and manner differ, most holding that the breath entered through her garment.

The verse describes Mary's reaction when she saw, in her seclusion, a man of perfect form standing before her. Fearing he meant her harm, she sought refuge in the Most Merciful and told him that if he feared God he should keep away. Most commentators identify him as Gabriel, sent in human form so that Mary could bear to hear him. Al-Tabari, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir report that she suspected he wanted her for immorality. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the conditional phrase as a reminder to him to fear God. Al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan explain that the sense is: since piety is hoped of you, I seek refuge in God from you, and piety should keep you from wrongdoing. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that the answer to the condition is implied. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi transmit from Ibn Abbas that Taqi was the name of a notorious sinner of that time, a view Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir judge weak. Abu Wa'il, cited in al-Bukhari, notes that Mary knew the pious person has understanding. Al-Sam'ani and Ibn Ashur stress that the phrase is meant to stir up piety. The verse highlights Mary's chastity and self-restraint, as she invokes God before anything else.

Gabriel tells Mary that he is the messenger of her Lord, sent to give her a pure boy, meaning one free from sin. The commentators agree that the messenger is Gabriel and that the gift is the child who would be created without a father. Mary feared that the man wanted to harm her, so she sought refuge in the Merciful. Abu Wa'il, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that "pious" here means one who fears God and restrains himself from wrongdoing, and that her words were a reminder of his piety. Ibn Abbas and others report that a notorious man named Taqi lived in that time, a view Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi regard as weak. The readings "li-ahaba" (that I may give) and "li-yahaba" (that He may give) differ: al-Tabari prefers the first because it matches the codices, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan explain that the gift is attributed to the messenger because he was its cause, through the breath into her garment, or because he announced it. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that both readings carry the same meaning. As for "zakiyyan", most take it to mean free from sin, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi also allow the sense of growing in goodness, and al-Razi notes that it implies the purity required for prophethood.

Mary asks the messenger who has announced a pure son how she could have a child when no man has touched her and she has not been unchaste. The commentators agree that she is asking how the child will come to be, whether through marriage or through a direct creation by God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, followed by Ibn 'Ashur, take the word "touch" as a euphemism for lawful marriage, and read her statement that she was not unchaste as a further denial of fornication, since contact can be lawful or unlawful. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that fornication is not expressed by euphemism and so limit the word to marriage. Al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi argue that the word covers both. On the term baghiyy, al-Mubarrad takes it as a form of baghawiy, while Ibn Jinni takes it as a form of fa'il, and al-Sha'rawi notes that it denotes a woman who offers herself to men and stresses its intensity. Most commentators agree on the angel's answer: "So it is, your Lord said: it is easy for Me," meaning that creating a son without a father is simple for God, that he will be a sign to people and a mercy from Him, and that the matter has already been decreed.

The commentators explain that this verse gives Gabriel's reply to Mary, who wondered how she could have a son when no man had touched her and she had not been unchaste. He tells her that it is as she says, but that her Lord has declared it easy for Him, and that the child will be a sign for people and a mercy from God, since the matter has been decreed. The commentators agree that the birth of Jesus without a father shows God's complete power, that the boy is a sign and a mercy for those who believe in him, and that the decree cannot be changed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take 'thus' to mean that the matter is exactly as she was told, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read it as confirming what came before. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the pronouns may refer either to the creation itself or to the child. On how the conception happened, Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi and others report that Gabriel breathed into the fold of her garment, while Ibn Kathir favours an ordinary pregnancy, and Ibn Abbas speaks of conception and birth happening almost at once. The commentators present these views without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that Mary conceived Jesus after the angel breathed into her garment, and that she then withdrew far from her people with the child in her womb. Most agree on the plain sense: she secluded herself at a distance, fearing what her family might think, and the pangs of labour drove her to the trunk of a palm tree, which they describe as a dry trunk. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that she wished she had died, out of shame before people, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that such a wish is permitted in a trial of this kind, unlike a wish for death caused by bodily harm. The duration of the pregnancy is disputed: Ibn Abbas and most scholars say nine months as with any woman, al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari mention six, seven or eight months, and Ibn Abbas also says that conception and birth occurred in a single hour. On the place of withdrawal, al-Suddi places it east of the prayer niche, Wahb ibn Munabbih at Bethlehem, and al-Zamakhshari behind a mountain or at the far end of the house. The commentators observe that the Qur'an does not specify these details and does not settle the matter between these views.

This verse describes the moment when the pains of labour forced Mary to lean against the trunk of a palm tree, and she wished she had died before this or had been a forgotten thing. The commentators agree that "ajā'ahā" means that the labour pains drove her to the tree, and that the trunk (jidh) was a dry palm trunk standing in the desert in the depth of winter, against which she leaned to bear the pain, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. As for the reason for her wish, al-Suddi, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir attribute it to shame before people and fear that they would think ill of her, while al-Mawardi and al-Razi add that righteous people used to say similar words when a trial became hard. Ibn Kathir concludes from this that wishing for death during a trial is permitted, whereas al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya distinguish this from the prohibition of wishing for death because of bodily harm.

The commentators agree that "nasyan mansiyyan" means something insignificant, discarded, that no one remembers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn 'Abbas that it means "I would not have existed", from 'Ikrima and Mujahid that it is a discarded menstrual cloth, and from al-Rabi' that it is a miscarriage. The readings vary between kasra and fatha, which the scholars regard as two dialects with the same meaning.

Ibn 'Ashur notes that the Arabs call neglected objects "ansa'", and that Mary wished to become a thing no one would remember among her people before reaching this state.

This verse describes how someone called out to Mary from below, after she had given birth, telling her not to grieve because her Lord had placed a small stream beneath her. The commentators differ on who spoke. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and 'Ikrima, among others, say it was Gabriel, who stood lower down at the foot of the mound. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd and Ubayy ibn Ka'b say it was Jesus himself, who spoke at his birth. Al-Tabari prefers the view that it was Jesus, since the pronoun in the preceding verses refers to him, while Ibn Kathir favours Ibn 'Abbas's view that it was Gabriel. As for the word sariyy, most exegetes, including al-Hasan's rivals, Ibn Zayd and the majority, take it to mean a small stream or rivulet; some report that Gabriel struck the ground with his foot and a spring of fresh water gushed forth. Al-Hasan and others understand the word as referring to Jesus, meaning a noble or honoured person, although al-Hasan is reported to have retracted this reading. Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that the comfort was not for lack of food or drink but for the miracle that would vindicate her before the people who accused her. A hadith attributed to the Prophet identifying the sariyy as a river is judged weak by Ibn Kathir and Ibn Hajar, and the sounder report is the saying of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, transmitted as a companion's statement.

The commentators explain that after the birth God commanded Mary to shake the trunk of the palm tree so that fresh, ripe dates would fall upon her, a sign of favour and a miracle meant to calm her heart and comfort her eyes, together with the order to eat and drink from the stream placed beneath her. Most agree that rutab janiyy means dates picked fresh at their proper time, and that shaking the trunk is a means commanded to her, even though God could have made the fruit fall without it; some draw from this that taking the means is compatible with reliance on God. They differ about the trunk: Ibn Abbas and others say it was dry and God revived it, Mujahid says it was an ajwa palm bearing fruit, and Wahb says it was a palm not bearing fruit at that season. They also differ about the sarriyy: most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it to be a stream or small river, while al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to be Jesus himself, and al-Tabari prefers the first reading. As for who called to her from below, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak said it was Gabriel, while Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr said it was Jesus, and al-Tabari favours the latter. Many report that dates are beneficial for a woman after childbirth, and that Mary was commanded to keep silent so that her son could speak on her behalf; some discuss whether a vow of silence is valid in our law, most holding that it is not.

This verse records that God commanded Mary, after giving birth beneath the palm trunk, to eat fresh dates, drink from the stream beneath her, and be content. If anyone asked her about the child, she was to say that she had vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, meaning silence, and would speak to no human that day. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, agree that sawm here means silence, that such a vow belonged to their earlier law and is not binding in Islamic law, and that these words were spoken by Jesus himself, as Ibn Zayd and Wahb ibn Munabbih report. They differ over who called to her from below: Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi name Gabriel, while Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr name Jesus, an view al-Razi prefers since the context concerns a newborn. On the word sari, most, including al-Bara' and Ibn Abbas, take it to mean a small stream, while al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to mean Jesus himself; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the stream. Linguistically, the verb tasaqqatu is read in several ways depending on whether the subject is the palm or the trunk, and janiyyan denotes a fresh date ready for picking. Some say Mary spoke with angels but not with humans, and that a gesture could serve as speech for some scholars, while others hold that she was to speak the words aloud.

The commentators explain that Mary, reassured by what God had told her about her innocence, returned to her people carrying her son Jesus. When they saw her with the child they rebuked her: "O Mary, you have brought something monstrous." Mujahid, Qatada and al-Sudi take "fariyyan" to mean great and dreadful, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash to mean strange and unprecedented, Sa'id ibn Mas'ada to mean fabricated, and al-Kalbi sees in it an allusion to fornication. On the timing of the birth, Ibn 'Abbas reports that she came back after forty days of postnatal purification, while al-Sudi and Wahb ibn Munabbih say she carried him at once. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that her relatives suspected her, and that her people, known for their righteousness, were deeply grieved. As for "O sister of Aaron", opinions differ: some take it as her full brother, others as a descendant of Aaron, brother of Moses, as one says "O brother of Tamim", others as a pious man of her community to whom she was compared, and others as a notorious sinner used to shame her. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of Mughira ibn Shu'ba in Sahih Muslim, in which the Prophet explained that people named themselves after their prophets and righteous forebears, a reading most commentators adopt. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as stressing that the offence seemed all the more shocking coming from such virtuous parents.

The commentators explain that these words were addressed to Mary by her people when she returned carrying the infant Jesus. They are a rebuke: her parents were righteous, so how could she have done such a thing? All agree that "a man of evil" means a man who commits immorality and that "unchaste" (baghiyy) means an adulteress. They differ on who Harun is. Qatada, Ka'b, Ibn Zayd and al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, as al-Tabari reports, take him to be a pious man among the Children of Israel who bore that name, and she was compared to him in piety; they cite the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ noted that this people named their children after their prophets and righteous men. Al-Suddi and those who follow him hold that he was Moses' brother, from whose line she descended, in the way one says "O brother of Tamim" to a man of that tribe. Others, such as al-Kalbi, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak, say he was her brother, or a notoriously immoral man to whom she was likened in mockery. Al-Tabari prefers the hadith view, while Ibn Kathir and al-Razi point out the many centuries separating Moses and Mary. Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that "brother" can mean resemblance or belonging to a group. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention that the offspring of righteous stock are usually righteous, which makes the alleged fault seem all the more shocking to her accusers.

This verse describes Mary's response when her people confronted her after she brought her child to them. She did not speak but gestured toward Jesus, asking them to address him, and they reacted with astonishment, asking how they could speak to someone still in the cradle. The commentators agree on the basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that Mary had vowed silence, which is why she only pointed, and that she trusted the infant to answer on her behalf. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the people felt her gesture was mocking, and found this more offensive than the accusation of immorality. There is some discussion of the grammar of the phrase «man kana fi al-mahd». Abu Ubayda and al-Farra considered «kana» superfluous or equivalent to «to be», al-Zajjaj read it as a conditional meaning «whoever may be in the cradle», and al-Zamakhshari offered a reading that describes a past situation. Al-Qurtubi also favoured the conditional sense. On the word «mahd», Qatada understood it as the mother's lap, while others took it to mean a cradle. These differences concern grammar and vocabulary rather than the overall meaning of the passage.

In this verse the infant Jesus declares that he is the servant of God, that God has given him the Book and made him a prophet. The commentators read this first statement as a refutation of those who would make him divine or the son of God, and as a defence of his mother Mary, who had been accused. They differ on when he spoke. Most, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, hold that he spoke as a baby with the reason of an adult, while Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi holds that he spoke like a youth who understands without yet being responsible. Others, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Shinqiti, read the past tense as a future, meaning that God had decreed he would receive the Book and be a prophet. The Book is usually taken to be the Gospel, though al-Razi also records the view that it is the Torah. On being blessed wherever he is, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report Mujahid saying useful to people, Sufyan saying a teacher of goodness, and others saying he commanded good and forbade evil. Prayer and almsgiving are most often read as the ritual prayer and the obligatory alms, though al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention purification from sins, and Ibn Kathir wonders how a man with no property could pay alms. Several commentators note that these words cleared Mary of the charge of adultery, and Malik is cited as holding that the verse refutes those who deny divine decree.

This verse records the words of Jesus, while still in the cradle, which God caused him to speak to clear his mother Mary of accusation. He says that he is a servant of God, that he was given the Book and made a prophet, and that God made him blessed wherever he is and enjoined on him prayer and zakat as long as he lives. Al-Tabari explains blessing as benefit, citing Mujahid who says it means one who benefits others, Sufyan who says it means one who teaches good, and others who say it means enjoining good and forbidding evil or meeting people's needs. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the word is general and includes all these meanings. On zakat, al-Tabari and al-Mawardi mention two possibilities: the alms due on wealth or the purification from sins. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi note that Jesus had no property, so the command is read as conditional, or as an instruction to increase in good. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that he spoke in the cradle and then returned to the speech of infants, while al-Razi argues that God made him fully grown and endowed with reason. The commentators agree that the speech affirms Jesus's servanthood against those who exalted him and clears his mother, and that prayer, alms and kindness to parents were enjoined on earlier communities. Ibn al-Qayyim understands blessing as abundant good that a person passes on to others through teaching, advice and guidance.

This verse records the words of Jesus, while still in the cradle, declaring that God made him dutiful toward his mother and did not make him a tyrant or a wretch. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain barran as kindness and humble service toward the mother, while al-Samani, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi describe it as honouring and serving one's parents. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take jabbar to mean an arrogant person who considers himself above others, and shaqiyy to mean one who disobeys his Lord. Al-Mawardi offers other readings, such as one who is ignorant of God's rulings or who refuses advice. Several commentators, including al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, cite a saying that an undutiful son is arrogant and wretched, though not all of them endorse it. Al-Zamakhshari reads the definite article in al-salam as an indirect curse on Mary's accusers, a view echoed by al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy. Al-Qurtubi notes that the verse shows prayer and almsgiving were obligatory for earlier nations. Al-Razi sees the mention of the mother as a way of clearing Mary's name, and al-Sha'rawi develops the same reading, explaining that Jesus wanted to dispel any doubt about his mother's purity.

This verse records Jesus' words in the cradle, after Mary had gestured towards him. He says that peace and safety from God are upon him on three occasions: the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive. The commentators agree on the core meaning. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that peace on the day of birth means protection from the Devil's prick that touches every newborn, that peace at death means safety from the squeeze of the grave or from unbelief that often occurs at the moment of death, and that peace on the day of resurrection means security from the terrors of that day. Ibn Kathir also notes that this affirmation of his servanthood refutes what the Christians attribute to him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the definite article in "al-salam" is generic and carries an implicit curse on Mary's enemies, as in the verse "and peace upon those who follow the guidance". Al-Razi also reports that some take it as referring back to the peace said over Yahya. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that God's peace differs from the peace a person wishes another, and that these three moments are those when a human most needs security. Al-Razi explains salam as safety and a request for protection. The differences concern the precise meaning of peace at death, whether it is protection from unbelief, from the grave's squeeze or from misery, and whether the article is generic or definite, and none of these scholars settles between the views.

This verse states that the one whose story has just been told, the child borne by Mary, is Jesus son of Mary, and that this account is a word of truth about which there is no doubt. The commentators read it as a rejection of two positions: that of the Jews, who said he was born outside lawful marriage and called him a sorcerer and a liar, and that of the Christians, who raised him to divinity or to sonship of God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the "word of truth" as the true report revealed to believers, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi allow that "al-Haqq" may refer to God himself, Jesus being called a word of God because he came into being through the divine command "Be" without a father.

On the reading, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "qawla" in the accusative, as a cognate object or praise, while the majority read the nominative, as predicate or apposition. Al-Tabari prefers the nominative, citing the agreement of the readers of Hijaz and Iraq. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note a reading in the second person, "tamtarun", attributed to some readers, which addresses the Jews and Christians directly.

The commentators agree that the verb "yamtarun" means doubting or disputing, and they note that the Christians split into several groups over Jesus, which Qatada describes in detail. Al-Mawardi records that the verb can mean both doubt and quarrel. The following phrase denies that God could take a son; al-Razi draws rational arguments from eternity and createdness, while others simply stress that such a thing is impossible for a God who creates by a single command.

This verse states that God is far above having a son, since a son implies need and imperfection, whereas when He decrees something He simply says « Be » and it is. The commentators place the verse within the words of Jesus, who rejects those who claim he is the son of God: Jesus is a created being whom God brought into existence by His word without a father, which proves no filiation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see it as a refutation of the Christians who made him the son of God or one of three. All agree that « Glory be to Him » is an absolute declaration of God's transcendence above such a claim. Al-Zamakhshari explains that « Be » is a figure for the speed with which the divine will is carried out, without effort or hardship, as al-Tabari also notes. On the reading of « wa-inna Allah rabbi wa-rabbukum », the readers of Medina and Basra read it with a fatha, linking it to what precedes, while the readers of Kufa read it with a kasra, beginning a new sentence; al-Tabari prefers the kasra. Al-Razi notes that the nature of God's word « kun » was debated between those who held it eternal and those who held it created, with no consensus reached. All agree on the final meaning: God is the Lord of all, He alone must be worshipped, and that is the straight path.

This verse, within the story of Jesus, states that God is the Lord of Jesus and of all people, so He alone must be worshipped, and that this is the straight path. Most commentators understand these as Jesus's words to his people: he is God's servant, and God is his Lord and theirs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy present the passage as a statement of monotheism in Jesus's own voice. Readers differed on the opening of the hamza in 'inna': al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the fatha as a causal clause, 'because God is my Lord and yours', while the kasra, the reading of Kufa and Syria, marks a fresh statement; al-Tabari prefers the kasra but accepts the fatha. Al-Razi notes that the command to worship follows the mention of lordship, which indicates that worship is owed because God is the one who nourishes and blesses creation. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur link the verse to what follows about the divisions among Christians over Jesus. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take the 'straight path' to mean belief in God's oneness, a way that leads to salvation. Commentators agree on this basic meaning without deciding between the readings.

This verse states that the parties among the People of the Book differed about Jesus after his situation had been made clear, and it threatens those who disbelieved with woe, al-wayl, at the sight of a tremendous day. The commentators agree that the parties are from among the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, and that the division arose from among themselves, as Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note. On who exactly they are, opinions differ: al-Kalbi and al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn al-Jawzi in one of his answers, identify them as Jews and Christians; Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify them with the three Christian groups, the Yaqubiyya, Nestorians and Melkites; a report from Ibn 'Abbas, repeated in al-Jalalayn, identifies them with the polytheists who banded against the Prophet. Qatada's reports describe a dispute that turned into fighting. As for the word mashhad, most take it as the Day of Judgment, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as the terror of the reckoning, the place or time of that spectacle, the testimony of angels, prophets and limbs against the wrongdoers, or what they said about Jesus and his mother. al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi say al-wayl is a valley in Hell, while Ibn 'Atiyya glosses it as grief and ruin. On the phrase 'hear them and see them', Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hayyan read it as an expression of wonder, while al-Hasan and Qatada say they will hear and see on that day but it will not benefit them.

This verse says that on the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers will hear and see far more keenly than they did in this world, yet this will bring them no benefit. The exclamative form has led commentators to say that their hearing and sight that day are astonishing, since they were deaf and blind to the truth in life. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, take it to mean the Day of Judgment. Qatada and al-Hasan explain that it means how well they will hear and see the guidance when it no longer serves them, while Ibn Zayd notes that in this world a veil covered their eyes and deafness filled their ears, and that on the Last Day they saw and heard without profiting. Al-Kalbi and others read it as a threat: they will hear and see what will distress them. Abu al-'Aliya reads it as an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ to make people hear and see the fate of these people and what awaits them. Al-Zamakhshari observes that using the phrase 'the wrongdoers' instead of a pronoun signals that no wrong is greater than theirs, since they neglected listening and looking when it would have benefited them. Nearly all agree that the wrongdoers are polytheists and disbelievers, and that their clear error in this world is their neglect of listening to and reflecting on the truth. Ibn Kathir also cites the authentic hadith in which death appears as a ram that is slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire, which marks the moment of anguish when the people of Paradise inherit their dwellings. Ibn Sa'di holds that they have no excuse, whether they are stubborn or content with their error without seeking the truth. The commentaries are not weighed against one another here.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to warn the polytheists of the Day of Regret, which most commentators identify with the Day of Resurrection, when every person regrets his conduct: the wrongdoer his misdeeds and the righteous his scant good deeds. It will be the time when the matter is decided between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, while in this world they are heedless of what awaits them and do not believe. The commentators agree that regret comes when the recompense becomes evident, but they differ on the date and on the meaning of the decided matter. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, relying on the authentic hadith, report that Death will be brought as a white-spotted ram between Paradise and the Fire and slaughtered, and it will be said to the people of Paradise, eternity without death, and to the people of the Fire, eternity without death, which increases the joy of the one and the sorrow of the other. Ibn Mas'ud, as reported by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, says that every soul will see its place in Paradise that it would have had if it had believed, and so will regret. Ibn Zayd holds that the Day of Regret is the whole Day of Resurrection. Muqatil takes the decided matter to be the decreeing of punishment, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand it as the end of the reckoning and the separation of the two groups. Al-Razi judges that the regret occurs in the hereafter and not in Paradise, since regret is a grief unbefitting the rewarded. Ibn Atiyya suggests the Day of Regret may be a general category covering many moments of regret. Al-Sha'rawi explains heedlessness as turning the mind away from clear evidence. Most commentators connect the phrase about heedlessness and unbelief with the present life.

This verse states that God is the true inheritor of the earth and of all upon it: when He causes its creatures to perish, no one will keep ownership or authority, and everyone will return to Him to be recompensed for their deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that this means the death of all the earth's inhabitants, with God remaining alone after them. Ibn 'Ashur reads the inheritance as a metaphor for the end of all shared human control, leaving God alone in charge, and sees the verse as a warning to polytheists who worship things that cannot benefit them.

The commentators broadly agree that the "Day of Regret" is the Day of Resurrection, when the wrongdoer regrets his misdeeds and the good-doer regrets how little good he did. Ibn Mas'ud reports that every soul will see the place in Paradise it could have had. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi link the day to the moment when judgement is complete and each group is sent to its abode. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of death brought as a white-spotted ram and slaughtered between Paradise and Hell, which others take as the meaning of the Day of Regret itself. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi are more cautious, suggesting it may be a general term for many moments of regret.

On the phrase "how much they hear and see", al-Hasan and Qatada take it as an expression of wonder at their state on the Day of Resurrection, when they hear and see but it no longer benefits them, while Abu al-Aliya takes it as an address to the Prophet to inform people of their fate. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Sa'di stress the contrast between worldly blindness and late clarity that brings no salvation.

God instructs His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to mention Abraham in the Book, and the commentators explain that the siddiq is one who is greatly truthful and who fully believes in God's unseen, His signs, His books and His messengers, while the prophet is one who receives revelation and holds an elevated rank. They agree that Abraham combined both sincerity and prophethood, and that mentioning him in the Qur'an means reciting his story to people and conveying it to them. The tafsirs report that Abraham addressed his father gently and affectionately: he asked why he worshipped idols that neither hear nor see and avail nothing, told him of knowledge that had reached him but not his father, invited him to follow him to a straight path, warned him not to obey Satan, who rebelled against the Most Merciful, and frightened him with the punishment of the Most Merciful and of becoming Satan's ally. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri read this as a call to monotheism and a prohibition of worshipping other than God. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi paused over the ta in (ya abati) and over the meaning of 'fear': Ibn 'Atiyya holds that fear is meant literally, since Abraham had not despaired of his father's faith, while al-Farra' takes it to mean 'knowing'. Al-Razi set out in detail the arguments against idol worship and explained that the account of Abraham, placed after those of Zechariah and Jesus, serves as proof of Muhammad's prophethood through its report of the unseen. The commentators also see the story as a consolation for the Prophet in the face of the opposition of his polytheist people.

God reminds His Prophet ﷺ of the story of Abraham, who said to his father, whom the commentators identify as Azar, rebuking him for worshipping idols that neither hear, nor see, nor avail him anything. The verse emphasises that worship belongs only to the One who is perfect and bestows favours. The commentators agree that Abraham addressed his father with gentleness and courtesy, opening with a question rather than a reproach. He then set out the knowledge that had come to him, asked his father to follow him so he could guide him to a straight path, forbade him to obey Satan, and warned him of the punishment of the Most Merciful. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the ta in 'O my father' as a substitute for the possessive suffix, while al-Farra' understands 'akhafu' to mean 'I know'. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn al-Qayyim highlight the delicacy of the address, which never belittles the father. The father's answer was harsh and threatening: Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean beating, al-Hasan stoning, al-Dahhak verbal abuse. On the phrase 'maliyyan' in 'abandon me for a while', most scholars read it as a long time, while Ibn 'Abbas read it as 'safe and sound', a view al-Tabari preferred. Abraham replied with a word of peace and a promise to seek forgiveness, which Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi place before it became clear that his father was an enemy of God.

This verse records Ibrahim's words to his father: O my father, God has given me knowledge that has not come to you, so follow me and I will guide you to a straight path, free of crookedness. The commentators note that Ibrahim neither calls his father extremely ignorant nor proclaims his own superior learning; he presents himself as a companion on the road who knows the way better, and addresses him gently. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi agree that this knowledge is knowledge of God, faith, and what concerns the hereafter, and that the straight path is the way that leads to salvation. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that the verb "fear" in the following verse may signify genuine fear, since Ibrahim had not yet despaired of his father's faith; al-Razi reports that al-Farra' reads it as "knowing", but he himself favours genuine fear. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the knowledge as what God granted him, whereas al-Zamakhshari takes it as knowledge of the way to the straight path. Al-Razi explains that the decisive argument is the rebuke for worshipping what neither hears nor sees, while the call to follow him is one of guidance rather than obligation. There is broad agreement that the passage relies on gentleness, tender appeals to fatherhood and repeated address, which al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn al-Qayyim present as a lesson in kindly and courteous speech.

This verse records Abraham's admonition to his father Azar: do not obey Satan by worshipping idols, for Satan has been disobedient to the Most Merciful. The commentators agree on the plain sense: one should not follow Satan in the enticements of polytheism, and Satan is presented as rebellious against God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that worshipping idols amounts in reality to obeying Satan, who commands it, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that this wording discredits idol worship more strongly by linking it to the enemy of God. On the word 'asiyyan', al-Tabari and al-Kisa'i take it to mean 'disobedient', while Ibn al-Jawzi treats it as a form of the active participle. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the name of the Most Merciful highlights how grave the disobedience is, since it is directed against the One who showers blessings. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim stress the gentle manner of the address, which opens with 'O my father' and proceeds with tenderness. On this verse the commentators largely agree, and no judgment is passed between them here.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, tells his father that he fears a punishment from the Most Merciful will befall him if he dies in disbelief, and that he would then become a companion of Satan in the fire. The commentators agree that this speech is marked by gentleness and courtesy: Ibrahim does not state that the punishment will certainly come, but uses an indefinite noun and the gentler verb "to touch," and he mentions Satan's companionship only afterwards. On the meaning of "fear," opinions differ: al-Tabari and al-Farra' take it to mean "knowing," while most, including al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, keep its ordinary sense, since Ibrahim had not despaired of his father's faith and was not certain that he would die in disbelief. As for the "walaya" (alliance) with Satan, many understand it as companionship in the fire and closeness to him, while others see it as divine abandonment, a bond in this life, or following Satan. Al-Razi notes that this alliance is worse than the punishment itself, by analogy with divine approval being greater than reward. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the speech forbids obeying Satan in worshipping idols, since obeying someone in disobedience to God amounts to worshipping him. The commentators also observe that the name "the Most Merciful" shows that the punishment is the consequence of disobedience, and that the father's harsh reply follows.

This verse records the reply of Ibrahim's father when his son urged him to abandon idol worship: he rebukes him for turning away from his gods and threatens, if he does not stop reviling them, to stone him, telling him to leave him alone for a long time. The commentators agree that the father worshipped idols and that these words are a threat. They differ on the meaning of stoning: al-Hasan and 'Ikrima took it as stones or killing, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Juraydj and Mujahid understood it as verbal abuse; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favoured this second view, and al-Razi also reports the view that it means driving him away with stones. As for 'leave me for a long while', Mujahid, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi read it as a long period or an age, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak read it as 'depart safe from my punishment', a reading al-Tabari preferred because it follows the preceding threat. Ibrahim replies 'Peace be upon you', which most scholars take as a parting and withdrawal rather than a greeting, while others see it as kindness and honour. He promises to seek forgiveness for him from God; the commentators differ on what this promise means, some saying it was a request for guidance and others a pledge made before he knew that God does not forgive unbelievers. Ibn Kathir notes that this plea was later abandoned once it became clear that his father was an enemy of God.

This passage records Abraham's reply to his father, who had threatened to stone him and banish him.
