He says, "Peace be upon you," meaning he will not harm him or oppose him further, and promises to ask his Lord to forgive him, since Allah has been gracious to him and answers his prayers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that this peace is a farewell and a parting rather than a greeting, and that the requested forgiveness means asking Allah to grant his father repentance and faith. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd explain hafiyy as kind or gentle, while others take it as generous, attentive or answering prayers. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that Abraham may not yet have known that his father would die an unbeliever, and al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari discuss whether seeking forgiveness for an unbeliever is permitted, with Zamakhshari holding that only revelation forbids it, not reason. Al-Qurtubi reports that Ibn 'Uyayna allowed greeting an unbeliever, a view he weighs against a hadith forbidding beginning Jews and Christians with the greeting. On the meaning of maliyyan, al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas read it as "safe and sound," while most commentators read it as a long time. Abraham then withdraws from his people and their idols, asking his Lord not to let him be wretched, a humble phrasing that implicitly points to the misery of those who worship idols.

This verse records Abraham's reply to his father, who had threatened to stone him and ordered him to leave. Abraham says "Peace be upon you," which the commentators read as a farewell and a parting, and he answers insult with kindness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take his promised forgiveness as a prayer that God guide his father to monotheism and forgive him, and they explain "hafiyyan" as gentle towards him and answering his supplications. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya stress kindness, tenderness and generosity instead. Most read the withdrawal as Abraham's migration to Syria, as reported by al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi. Al-Zamakhshari sees the supplication as worship and the word "perhaps" as humility that hints at the wretchedness of his people. The commentators differ on the greeting: the majority, with al-Tabari, read it as a pledge of safety rather than a welcome, while al-Naqqash reads it as a patient man addressing a fool. On the promised forgiveness, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi debate whether it came before the prohibition on praying for unbelievers became known, while Ibn Kathir links it to a practice later abrogated. On the phrase "for a long time" in the parting, al-Hasan and Mujahid take it as a long period, while Ibn Abbas takes it as leaving him unharmed. Almost all see the gift of Isaac and Jacob as compensation for the family he left, and the "tongue of truthfulness" as lasting praise.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the story of Abraham after he withdrew from his father, his people, and what they worshipped besides Allah. He emigrated from them, and Allah compensated him with Isaac and Jacob, making each of them a prophet. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the gift came after the separation and migration, and that Jacob is the son of Isaac. The word 'kullan' means each of them. As for divine mercy, al-Hasan takes it to mean prophethood, al-Kalbi wealth and children, and others, such as Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, a blessing both religious and worldly. On the 'tongue of truth that is elevated', they all agree it is a lasting good reputation, as Ibn Abbas, Malik ibn Anas and al-Suddi said, with 'tongue' standing for what is spoken and its height reflecting that all religions praise them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi add that tongue may also mean a message or the Arabic language. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur report that Abraham rejoiced to see his grandson Jacob. Al-Alusi and al-Shawkani lean toward Ishmael being the first gift, but the majority sees the order here as showing the greatness of the reward for emigration.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to Abraham after he withdrew from his people and from what they worshipped besides God. In compensation, God gave him Isaac and his grandson Jacob, made each of them a prophet, and then granted them mercy from Him. Most commentators understand this mercy as wealth, children and abundant provision, though al-Hasan takes it to mean prophethood and others add the Book or any worldly and religious good. Regarding the phrase tongue of truthfulness on high, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by Ibn Abi Talha, read it as a lofty, lasting good reputation that people of all religions speak of them. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari also cite a reading in which tongue means message, so that they were made honoured messengers, and al-Mawardi adds the possibility of fulfilling promises. Ibn Ashur and Abu Hayyan note that the loftiness of this praise points to its prestige and its endurance through the ages. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud observe that tongue stands for the praise uttered by it, just as hand stands for a gift, and that attributing it to truthfulness shows the praise is deserved. Ibn al-Qayyim links it to the truthfulness of those who receive it. All agree that this blessing was a reward to Abraham for his migration and his separation from his people for God's sake.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to recount in the Book the story of Moses, describing him as sincere in devotion and as both a messenger and a prophet. The commentators agree that the word "mukhlis" means one who devotes his worship to God alone and submits himself wholly to Him, and that messengerhood and prophethood are two qualities God joined in him. The readings differ: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "mukhlisan" with a kasra, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read "mukhlaṣan" with a fatha. The first group takes it to mean that Moses sincerely dedicated himself to God, the second that God chose and purified him. Al-Tabari judges that Moses was sincere both to God and to his mission, and that either reading is correct. Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy distinguish the messenger, who bears a Book, from the prophet, who receives revelation without being commanded to convey it. Regarding the call from "the blessed right side of the mountain", Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain it as Moses' right, since a mountain has no right side. Most understand "najiyyan" as one who converses in private, while Ibn 'Abbas and others report that he was brought so close that he heard the scratching of the pen, and Qatada links the word to being saved through sincerity. Finally, God granted him his brother Aaron as a prophet in answer to his request, as Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note.

This verse recalls that God called Moses from the right side of Mount Tur, meaning the side on Moses' right as he approached the mountain, since the mountain itself has no right or left. God then brought him near in an honouring way, speaking with him intimately as one speaks in confidence. The commentators agree that this was a direct speech of God to Moses and that the drawing near was one of rank and honour. The word najiyy refers to one who converses privately. On what this nearness meant, opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others report, through Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliya, that Moses was lifted until he heard the scratching of the pen writing the Torah, while al-Razi, following al-Qadi, judges that the closer meaning is nearness of station. Al-Mawardi also mentions a reading that the word means elevated, and Qatada explains it as one saved through his truthfulness, a view Ibn Atiyya considers weak. Regarding the following phrase, Ibn Abbas, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that Aaron was older than Moses and that the gift was prophethood, granted in answer to Moses' request that his brother strengthen him. Al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari also note that every messenger is a prophet but not every prophet a messenger, while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur stress the distinction between the two terms.

The commentators explain that God brought Moses close and spoke with him in intimate conversation from the right side of the mount, and then granted him, out of His mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet. Most read this as the answer to Moses' prayer that his brother be made a helper and minister in his mission. Ibn 'Abbas, reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, states that Aaron was older than Moses, so the gift concerns his prophethood rather than his person. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note that "min rahmatina" may mean "because of Our mercy" or "part of Our mercy", and that "his brother" is then an object or an appositive depending on this reading; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy also record these readings. Ibn 'Ashur explains that Aaron's support consisted of speaking on Moses' behalf, since Moses had a speech impediment. Al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi connect the gift to the mission, citing passages in Surah Ta-Ha and Surah al-Qasas. All agree that Aaron is a prophet and that this prophethood is a divine gift that cannot be earned by devotion alone.

God tells His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to mention Isma'il in the Book, describing him as true to his promise and as a messenger and prophet. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, identify him as Isma'il son of Ibrahim, which is the majority view; a minority opinion, reported by al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi, holds that he was Isma'il son of Hizqil, another prophet. All agree that keeping one's word is praiseworthy, while breaking a promise is a trait of hypocrites. The commentators give several examples of his faithfulness: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi tell of the man he arranged to meet and waited for, whether for a day and a night, three days, or a full year according to other reports. The greatest proof is his promise to his father to be patient in the sacrifice, cited by al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. Ibn al-Jawzi explains that this quality was singled out because he endured more than other prophets to keep his commitments, and al-Razi notes that it applies both to his dealings with God and with people. On the mention of his prophethood and mission, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shawkani say he was sent to the tribe of Jurhum, and some, including al-Alusi, argue that a messenger need not bring his own law, since the descendants of Ibrahim followed his. Regarding the command to his family to pray and give alms, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take his family to be his household, whom he taught first so they would set an example, whereas others, such as al-Hasan and Ibn Juzayy, understand his people or community as a whole. Finally, God describes him as pleasing to his Lord, which al-Razi and Ibn Kathir read as a sign of his perfect uprightness in word and deed.

The commentators explain that this verse praises Ishmael, peace be upon him, for commanding his family to pray and to give zakat, and for being pleasing to his Lord. Al-Tabari says that he commanded them to establish prayer and pay zakat, and that he was praiseworthy in what his Lord imposed on him, never falling short in obedience. Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, take 'his family' to mean his people and community, since prophets are the fathers of their nations; al-Hasan and al-Nasafi likewise take it as his whole community, and Ibn Mas'ud's reading 'his people' supports this. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi add that he began with his own household so that they would be a model for those who followed, and that religious benefit to them takes priority. Al-Razi notes that zakat may mean the obligatory charity or sincerity, and that the command may be a recommendation. As for 'pleasing', most understand it as one who persisted in obedience and whom God chose for prophethood, and al-Razi regards it as the highest praise. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also connect the verse to Ishmael's faithfulness to his promises, as he waited patiently for a man with whom he had made an appointment. Some commentators suggested this is Ishmael son of Hizqil, but the majority hold that he is the son of Abraham.

God instructs His Prophet to mention Idris in the Book, describing him as a man of great truthfulness and a prophet to whom revelation was given. The commentators agree that Idris was one of the forefathers of Noah, that he was the first to write with the pen, the first to sew and wear stitched garments, and the first to study astronomy and calculation. On the phrase 'and We raised him to a lofty station,' opinions differ. Al-Hasan and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani took it to mean high rank and the dignity of prophethood, a view Ibn Juzayy considers the more established, while most exegetes understood a literal elevation to the heavens. As to the place, Anas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mujahid, Abu al-Aliya and Ka'b al-Ahbar said the fourth heaven, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said the sixth, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam said Paradise. On his death, Muqatil held that he died in the heavens, whereas Mujahid and others held that he did not die, like Jesus. Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Kathir relay narratives from Ka'b and Wahb about the reason for his elevation and the taking of his soul, which Ibn Kathir classes among the Israelite reports, some of which are considered questionable. Some identify Idris with Elias, a view attributed to Ibn Mas'ud.

The Qur'an praises Idris as a truthful man and a prophet, and says that God raised him to a high place. The commentators differ on what this elevation means. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi, understand a literal raising up to heaven, relying on the report of the Night Journey transmitted through Anas ibn Malik and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, in which the Prophet saw Idris in the fourth heaven. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak place him in the sixth heaven, and Zayd ibn Aslam says he is in Paradise. Others, such as al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, take it to mean an elevation of rank, the nobility of prophethood and nearness to God. On his death, the views differ: Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi report that he died in heaven, and accounts attributed to Ka'b al-Ahbar and Ibn 'Abbas describe how his soul was taken there, while Mujahid says he was raised without dying, like Jesus. Ibn Kathir considers these accounts to come from Israelite traditions and to contain strange elements. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, note that Idris is regarded as the first to write with a pen, the first to sew garments and the first to study the stars and calculation. Al-Razi observes that an elevation linked to a place is usually taken as spatial, which lends weight to the literal reading.

This verse refers to the prophets named in Surat Maryam, drawn from the descendants of Adam, those carried with Noah in the ark, and the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and states that God favored, guided and chose them, and that when the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them they fell down prostrate and weeping. Al-Tabari and al-Sudi identify the lineages individually: Idris from the offspring of Adam, Abraham among those carried with Noah, Isaac, Jacob and Ishmael from Abraham's line, and Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John and Jesus from Israel's line. Ibn Kathir holds that the verse means the prophets as a whole and not only those in this sura, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the Israelite line includes Jesus through his mother Mary. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy note that Idris was an ancestor of Noah, and Ibn Kathir reports a view that he was among the prophets of Israel. On the prostration and weeping, the commentators agree that they express humility and fear of God. Al-Mawardi distinguishes prostration as hope from weeping as awe, and al-Razi cites the prophetic saying to recite the Quran and weep or feign weeping. Many derive the recommended prostration of recitation from the verse, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi noting that it is not clearly obligatory, and they recall that Omar prostrated on reciting it and asked where the weeping was. Ibn Atiyya holds the reading bikiyyan with kasra to be a verbal noun, while most treat it as the plural of baki.

The commentators explain that this verse describes a generation that came after the prophets mentioned in the surah, a bad successor who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, and whose fate is to meet "ghayy", meaning loss and evil. On the meaning of neglecting the prayer, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Mujahid and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, as reported by al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir, took it to mean delaying the prayer beyond its time, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi also mention performing it without its conditions or abandoning it. Al-Tabari, who favours total abandonment, relies on the exception that follows in the verse. The desires are mostly understood as sins such as drinking wine, fornication and usury, and Ali ibn Abi Talib described them through lavish building, showy mounts and conspicuous clothing.

Opinions differ on who this successor generation is. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil identify them as the Jews, al-Suddi as the Jews and Christians, and Mujahid, Qatada, Ata and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi as people of this community at the end of time. Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti hold that the wording is general and covers any group that neglects the prayer and follows its desires. Regarding "ghayy", Ibn Mas'ud and Ka'b take it as a valley or river in hell, Ibn Abbas as ruin, Ibn Zayd as evil or error, and al-Zamakhshari as the recompense of error.

The exception that follows, opening the way to forgiveness for whoever repents, believes and does good, is understood by all as a door left open for repentance. The commentators then describe the Gardens of Eden, where no idle talk is heard but only greetings of peace, and where provision comes morning and evening according to what the Arabs knew on earth.

This verse describes a later generation of evil successors who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, and who will meet ghayy, which many commentators explain as a valley in Hell. It then makes an exception for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds: they will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least. The commentators differ on who these successors are. Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Suddi say they were the Jews, while Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir say they are groups from this community who will appear at the end of time, a view supported by a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. On the meaning of neglecting the prayer, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz understood it as delaying it beyond its time, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi note that it may mean abandoning it altogether, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi consider the verse as addressing disbelievers. Al-Tabari reads the exception as linked to the one who turned from disbelief, while al-Razi observes that faith and good deeds are listed separately, implying they are distinct. Al-Zamakhshari explains that not being wronged means that no part of the reward is withheld because of past disbelief. Ibn Kathir, following al-Tabari, adds that repentance wipes out what came before it. The verse then speaks of the Gardens of Eden that the Merciful promised to His servants unseen, and His promise will certainly come to pass.

This verse describes the gardens that those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds will enter: the Gardens of Eden, that is, lasting dwellings, which the All-Merciful promised to His servants although they had not seen them, believing in the unseen. The commentators agree that the phrase "ma'tiyyan" means that its recipients will certainly come to it, since God's promise never fails. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also report the view of the Kufan grammarians that the word carries the sense of "coming", since whatever reaches you, you reach as well. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan treat "Adn" as a proper name for the abode of permanence or the land of Paradise, while al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take the gardens as an apposition to "the Garden". In the next verse, most scholars hold that the people of Paradise hear no idle talk, only greetings, whether from the angels or from one another. There is disagreement about provision "morning and evening": al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as the measure of the daily meals of this world, since the Arabs regarded morning and evening meals as the height of comfort; Mujahid says there is no morning or evening, but that people receive what they desire; Qatada speaks of two periods of light with no night; al-Razi understands it as continuous provision. Finally, the statement that the pious inherit this Garden is explained by al-Tabari as the granting of dwellings, and by al-Razi as a metaphor for an inheritance passed to an heir.

This verse describes the condition of the people of Paradise: they hear no vain or idle speech there, only the greeting of peace. Most commentators read the exception as disconnected, meaning 'but they hear a word of peace'. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as the angels' greeting to the believers and their greeting to one another, while Muqatil focuses on the angels' salutation. Al-Mawardi also mentions the sense of mere safety. Some, such as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, read the exception as connected, citing Nabigha's verse that praises through an apparent fault. As for the provision 'morning and evening', most explain it as the measure of those two times of day known in worldly life, since Paradise has neither night nor day but light. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that al-Hasan and Qatada said the Arabs regarded a morning and an evening meal as the height of comfort, so the verse speaks in their terms. Mujahid holds that they receive what they desire without fixed times. Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress the continuity of this provision. Several transmitters report that the inhabitants know night from day by the lowering and raising of veils. All agree on the lasting nature of these blessings and the absence of hurtful speech in Paradise.

This verse refers to the Garden described in the preceding verses, the Gardens of Eden, and states that God gives it as an inheritance to those of His servants who are God-fearing. The commentators agree that piety is the condition for inheriting it. As to the meaning of inheritance, they offer two closely related readings. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi report that believers receive the dwellings that would have belonged to the people of the Fire had they believed. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take the word as a metaphor: God preserves the Garden for the pious, just as an heir keeps a dead man's wealth, since their deeds end and their fruit, the Garden, remains. Al-Razi adds that piety means avoiding sins and not neglecting obligations. Al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi also note that disbelief is treated as a kind of spiritual death, so believers inherit the places of disbelievers. Al-Sha'rawi holds that every person has a place in Paradise and one in Hell, and that when the people of the Fire enter Hell, their places in Paradise pass to the people of Paradise. Al-Shinqiti, while accepting a related hadith, argues that the verse refers to the believers' own places. In recitation, the common reading is nuwrithu, while Ya'qub reads nuwarrithu. This summary presents these views without judging between them.

This verse states that the descent of the angels, including Gabriel, happens only by God's command, and that God alone owns what is before us, behind us, and between these. The commentators report that it was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ was waiting for Gabriel, who had delayed his visit, and the Prophet asked why he did not come more often, as related by al-Bukhari through Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others also link the delay to the Quraysh's questions about the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn and the Spirit, with the length of the delay reported as twelve nights, fifteen days, or forty days. On the meaning of 'before us' and 'behind us' the scholars differ. Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj take what is before us as the Hereafter and what is behind us as this world, while Mujahid reverses this. Abu al-'Aliya and others take the middle to be the period between the two blasts of the trumpet, while others understand it as the interval between this world and the next. Al-Tabari prefers the Hereafter as what is ahead, since Arabic usage applies this to what has not yet come. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi also report that these words may be spoken by the people of Paradise as they enter it. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi read the verse as stating that the angels are bound by God's will in every movement. As for 'your Lord was not forgetful', some render it as 'your Lord did not abandon you', while others take it as 'your Lord is not forgetful', and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the latter sense.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God is the Lord of the heavens, the earth and everything between them, meaning their Creator, their Owner and the one who disposes of them, and therefore commands the Prophet to worship Him alone and to persevere in that worship despite its hardships. Most of them, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, agree that the word "namesake" (samiyyan) means a like, an equal or a peer, so that nothing is comparable to God. Al-Kalbi and others add that it means one who bears God's name: no one has ever been named Allah, and Ibn Abbas adds that no one bears the name Ar-Rahman besides Him. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari mainly keep the sense of a peer, while al-Razi links the matter to the countless blessings God bestows, which justify the greatest worship. As for the verb "persevere", al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that it takes the preposition lam because it carries the sense of standing firm against trials, as a fighter stands before his opponent. Several commentators report that the verse belongs to the context of the delay in revelation to the Prophet, when Gabriel explained that he descends only by God's command. Reports differ on how long that delay lasted. Ibn Atiyya notes that the verse reminds us that angels act only by divine order. These explanations, though phrased differently, largely converge.

This verse reports the words of the one who denies resurrection and finds it unlikely that he will be brought back alive once he has become dust. The commentators agree that the speaker is a disbeliever, and the tone is one of denial and mockery, as Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi point out. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that 'al-insan' may denote the whole human species, of which only some utter such words, in the way one says 'the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so' when only one of them did. Others, such as al-Wahidi cited by al-Qurtubi, name Ubayy ibn Khalaf as the speaker, while al-Mahdawi and Ibn Ashur mention al-Walid ibn al-Mughira or al-As ibn Wa'il. The divine reply calls the speaker to reflect on his first creation: the One who created him from nothing can recreate him, as Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress. Readers differ on 'yadhkuru': Nafi, Ibn Amir and Asim read it unshadda, while most read the doubled form; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi consider the doubled form preferable without rejecting the other. On the phrase 'there is none of you but will approach it', al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi relay several views: that all will enter Hell, that it means crossing the bridge over it, or merely coming near it. They agree that the righteous are saved and the wrongdoers are left within.

This verse reports the words of the man who denies the resurrection and wonders whether he will be brought out alive after death. God answers that he should remember that He created him before, when he was nothing, and that the One who created him from nothing can bring him back. The commentators agree on the general reasoning, but differ on who is meant. Al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the word "man" refers to the whole category, even though only some of them said it, in the way one says "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so". Others, such as al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, report that a specific person is meant, namely Ubayy ibn Khalaf, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira or al-As ibn Wa'il, depending on the report. On the reading of "yadhkuru", al-Tabari prefers the doubled form "yadhdhakkaru" in the sense of reflecting, while Nafi, Ibn Amir and Asim read the single form, meaning to remember. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur explain that the surprise lies in forgetting the first creation, which is more striking than the second, because the first brings something from nothing, whereas the second assembles existing parts. Ibn Kathir sees in this a proof from the beginning to establish the resurrection. The following verses announce the gathering of the disbelievers with their devils, their being brought kneeling around Hell, and then the separation of groups according to their rebellion. On the meaning of "jithiyyan", Ibn Abbas says groups or seated, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak say on their knees, and al-Suddi says standing on their knees because of the cramped space. On the verse about passing over Hell (warud), most hold it means entering it, while others take it to mean crossing the bridge or merely approaching. These differences concern details and do not touch the central affirmation of resurrection and judgment.

God swears by the Lord of His Prophet ﷺ that He will gather the deniers of resurrection together with their devils, and then bring them around Hell on their knees, overwhelmed by terror and humiliation. The commentators see this verse as a continuation of the threat against the disbelievers who found it hard to believe they would be brought back to life after death. The word «and the devils» is read by most as meaning «together with», so that each unbeliever is chained alongside his own devil, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Kalbi report. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take «kneeling» to mean sitting or kneeling, whereas al-Suddi and al-Hasan say they stand on their knees because of the cramped space, and Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' explain it as gathering in groups. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that kneeling was the usual posture at moments of judgement, and that the gathering around Hell lets believers see what God saved them from, while the wicked see their fate. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the posture expresses abasement rather than submission. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi observe that «al-insan» means the disbelievers, and they connect the revelation to Ubayy ibn Khalaf, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira or al-As ibn Wa'il. The commentators agree on the meaning of the gathering itself and differ mainly on the form of kneeling and its timing.

This verse says that after God gathers those who denied the resurrection together with their devils around Hell, kneeling, He will single out from every group united in disbelief the one most insolent against the Most Merciful, and begin with him. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid explain that a shi'a is a community or a group bound together, Ibn Abbas reading 'utiyy as boldness and Mujahid as wickedness or disbelief. Al-Tabari reports through Abu al-Ahwas, Ibn Jurayj and others that the greatest in sin and the leaders of evil are taken first. Al-Kalbi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi also take the intended people to be the leaders of error, whose punishment is multiplied because they both misled and were misled. Grammarians disagree on the case of 'ayyuhum': Sibawayh holds it is built on a final damma, al-Khalil that it is a nominative by quotation, and Yunus that the verb is suspended; al-Zajjaj prefers al-Khalil's view, while Ibn 'Atiyya and others criticise Sibawayh. The next verse, about God knowing who deserves to burn most, is read by Ibn Kathir as meaning that followers are punished after their leaders, and by others as God knowing who most deserves to be burned.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the description of the disbelievers in resurrection gathered with their devils around hell, kneeling. God will then draw out from every group the one most defiant against the Most Merciful, and affirms that He knows best who deserves most to burn in the Fire. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil take "most deserving of it" to mean most deserving of entering it. Ibn Jurayj, in one report, understands eternal dwelling, but al-Tabari rejects this since all disbelievers abide there, and he takes it to mean certain levels of hell.

Most exegetes agree that the drawing out means separating the most stubborn rebels from each group so they are cast first into the Fire. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Kalbi say the greatest offenders come first, while Ibn Jurayj and Qatada identify them as the leaders of evil. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that the leaders of the factions are meant, since their punishment is doubled for misleading others.

The grammarians quoted differ on the grammar of "ayyuhum". Sibawayh holds it is indeclinable because the start of its relative clause has been dropped, al-Khalil treats it as nominative by quotation, and Yunus takes the verb as suspended. Al-Farra' and al-Mahdawi read the verb as meaning a call.

The commentators explain that none of mankind, righteous or wicked, will escape the Fire; this is a decree that God has made binding upon Himself and that must certainly come to pass. The meaning of 'wurud' (coming to, or approaching) is where opinions diverge. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and Khalid ibn Ma'dan take it to mean entering the Fire, which will become cool and safe for believers, as it was for Abraham, so that they pass through it unharmed; al-Tabari favours this reading. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatada understand it as crossing the bridge (as-sirat) laid over Hell, which people cross at varying speeds according to their deeds. 'Ikrima and Sa'id ibn Jubayr restrict the verse to disbelievers. Others, such as Mujahid, take it to mean the fever a believer suffers in this world. As for 'a decree decided', Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj read it as 'a judgement', while Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada read it as a binding oath. The scholars do not settle the meaning of 'wurud' but report each view with its evidence. All agree that the God-fearing will be saved and the wrongdoers left kneeling within the Fire.

This verse states that all people will come to Hell, after which God will save the righteous and leave the wrongdoers there, kneeling. The commentators differ on the meaning of "wurud" (coming to it). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean passing over the Sirat, the bridge laid over Hell, where people cross according to their deeds, some saved and others falling in. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud give a similar reading, while Ibn 'Abbas also noted that the word can mean merely drawing near, as in the account of Madyan's water. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand it as standing around Hell. Others, including Ibn 'Abbas in another transmission, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari, hold that wurud means entering: the fire then becomes cool and safe for believers, as it was for Ibrahim, a report transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah. Mujahid explains it as the fever a believer suffers in this world. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the address may be only to disbelievers, the righteous being led to Paradise without entering the fire. Several works cite the hadith of Hafsa and Umm Mubashshir about the people of Badr and Hudaybiyya, in which the Prophet replies: "Be quiet; then We shall save those who were righteous." The wrongdoers are usually identified as disbelievers and polytheists. The word "jithiyyan" is explained by al-Hasan and Mujahid as "on their knees", by Ibn 'Abbas as "seated", and by others as "in groups". The commentators do not settle between these readings.

God reports that when clear verses of the Qur'an were recited to the disbelievers, they boasted to the believers: which of the two groups is better in station (maqam) and finer in assembly (nadi)? The commentators agree on the plain sense: maqam is the place of dwelling or standing, and nadi is the gathering place where people meet, which al-Tabari illustrates with a verse of Hatim al-Ta'i. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid report that the polytheists mocked the poverty of the believers, their rough living and worn clothes, while they themselves perfumed and adorned themselves; they took worldly prosperity as a sign of divine favour, a reasoning that Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di call a flawed argument. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi place the occasion of revelation among the Quraysh, notably al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note differing readings of the word maqaman, read with a fatha by most and with a damma by Ibn Kathir, who takes it as the dwelling place. The divine answer recalls earlier generations that were destroyed although they had greater wealth and finer appearance. Most exegetes take athath as furnishings and goods and ri'yan as outward appearance, while al-Hasan understands it as forms. The commentators conclude that the respite given to the misguided is a test and a delay, and that lasting good deeds are better in reward and in outcome.

The verse reports that when the clear verses of the Qur'an were recited to the disbelievers, they boasted to the believers: which of the two groups is better in standing and in assembly? God answers that many generations before them, which were finer in goods and appearance, were destroyed. The commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, agree that athath means goods and household furnishings or wealth, and that ri'y means outward appearance and splendour. Maqam means dwelling place or station, and nadi means the gathering place of a people. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi discuss the readings: the hamzated reading comes from sight, while the unhamzated reading may come from sight with the hamza changed, or from ri, meaning abundance and fresh well-being. A reading with zay means adornment and bearing. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di see the verse as refuting the claim that worldly prosperity proves divine favour, since God destroyed peoples who were more prosperous. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi describe the argument as a reversal of realities. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi relate that the Quraysh dressed and perfumed themselves while mocking poor believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the phrase 'let the Merciful extend his term' as a respite that leads to punishment, in this world or on the Last Day.

This verse says that whoever remains in error, the Most Merciful lets him continue in his misguidance for a long time, until he sees what he has been promised, either the punishment or the Hour, and then he will know who is worse in position and weaker in followers. It answers the claim of the disbelievers that they are better in station and finer in their gatherings. Most commentators agree that the imperative form of the first phrase conveys a fact: God leaves the misguided person in his error and prolongs it. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, explains that God leaves him in his rebellion, and Ibn Kathir follows this reading. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take the command as an emphasis that this respite is certain, in order to cut off the excuses of the one who strays, while Ibn al-Jawzi, citing Ibn al-Anbari, also allows that it is a supplication. Abu Hayyan considers it very unlikely that 'until' should be read as a mere supplication. The commentators agree that 'worse in position' answers 'better in station' and 'weaker in followers' answers 'finer in gathering', since the nadi is the assembly that brings together the notables and their supporters. On the punishment, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as killing and capture in this world, al-Razi offers several meanings including the punishment of the grave and the battle of Badr, and al-Baydawi chooses the domination of the Muslims over them. On the Hour, most take it as the Day of Resurrection. Finally, the commentators note that guidance increases for those who are rightly guided, and that the lasting good deeds are better in reward and in outcome, though they do not agree on what these are, some identifying them with faith and righteous deeds, others with glorifications and invocations.

This verse states that God increases in guidance those who are already rightly guided, and that lasting good deeds are better in reward and in outcome with their Lord, in contrast to what the disbelievers boast of: wealth, furnishings and gatherings. The commentators agree that the increase in guidance means the believer's steadfastness, growing certainty and success in good works. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain it as an increase in faith as obligations and verses are revealed, while Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di include beneficial knowledge and righteous action. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi also report, through al-Kalbi and Muqatil, that it can mean believing in the abrogating text after the abrogated one. On the lasting good deeds, opinions differ: al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take them as the deeds of the Hereafter or all acts of worship, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas identify them with the five daily prayers, and Ibn al-Jawzi links them to the obligatory duties. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu al-Darda about glorifying, praising and affirming God's oneness. Al-Razi prefers that they are faith and all good deeds, since their benefit endures. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the comparative of superiority as sarcasm, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi understand it as absolute superiority. Al-Shinqiti suggests that the good a disbeliever receives in this world may be what is compared with the believer's final reward.

In this verse God addresses His Prophet ﷺ in astonishment at a man who denied Our signs and claimed he would be given wealth and children. The commentators agree that this refers to al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, and they report the occasion of revelation recorded in al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the two Sahihs: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, a smith, asked al-As for a debt, and al-As replied that he would pay only if Khabbab rejected Muhammad. When Khabbab refused, al-As said that if he were raised after death he would have wealth and children and would then pay. The verse asks, "Have you considered him who has risen to the unseen, or taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" Qatada explains the covenant as a righteous deed sent ahead, al-Kalbi as a divine promise of Paradise, Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b as the testimony of faith, and Ibn Kathir as a binding pledge. The reply "No!" follows: his words will be recorded and he will be requited for them, his punishment will be extended, he will be stripped of what he had, and he will come before God alone. On the reading of "wuldan", al-Tabari and most scholars hold that the vowelled and unvowelled forms are two dialects with the same meaning, while others take one as plural and the other as singular. On "la-utayanna", most read it as referring to this world, whereas al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it as mockery concerning Paradise. Ibn al-Jawzi leans toward the latter on the basis of the reports, while Ibn Kathir follows the majority view.

This verse records the boast of a disbeliever, identified by most commentators as al-'As ibn Wa'il, who told Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, to whom he owed a debt, that he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter. The rhetorical question asks whether he has gained knowledge of the unseen or has made a covenant with the Most Merciful. The commentators agree that these are the only two ways to know such a thing, and that he has neither, so the answer is negative, and the word "kalla" serves as a rebuke.

On the meaning of "covenant", Qatada takes it as a righteous deed already done, Ibn 'Abbas as the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and al-Kalbi as a pledge from God to admit him to Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy explain that his claim may refer to this world or to the Hereafter. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read "We shall inherit what he says" as God stripping him of his wealth and children, while others take it as God withholding what he hoped for and giving it to others. The phrase "he will come to Us alone" means he will arrive with nothing. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also note the reading "wuldan" with a damma, which al-Tabari and others treat as a synonym of the fatha form, while Abu Hayyan reports it as a plural.

This passage answers the claim of the disbelieving man who expected to be given wealth and children in the afterlife. The commentators read "kalla" as a rejection of that claim: he has not gained knowledge of the unseen, nor made a covenant with the Most Merciful. On "We shall record what he says," al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that his words are preserved in order to be requited, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it either as making him aware that his words were recorded or as a threat of retribution. All agree that "We shall extend for him the punishment" means increasing his torment, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi describing it as punishment added to punishment, while others understand a prolonging of its duration. On "We shall inherit from him what he speaks of," most, including Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, understand the stripping away of the wealth and children he hoped for, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi, and al-Farra' hold that they will be given to other believers. Finally, "he will come to Us alone" refers to the Day of Resurrection, without wealth or children. Several reports link the verse to al-'As ibn Wa'il over a debt owed to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, while al-Hasan attributes it to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, the first view being the more widely held.

This verse states that God will record what this disbeliever says, who claimed he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter, and that He will increase his punishment. God will take away what he claimed to have, and he will come to Him alone, without wealth or children. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the word 'inheriting' here means God will strip him of the wealth and children he had, citing Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as seizing the wealth and children themselves, while Ibn Ashur sees it as a figure for loss, and even suggests that his sons would become Muslims.

There is broad agreement that 'alone' (fardan) means without wealth or children. Al-Mawardi adds that it may mean without a helper or protector, a view also noted by al-Alusi. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi likewise describe a state of arriving empty-handed. Al-Razi holds that what he hoped for will never come to pass.

On the occasion of revelation, the most cited report, transmitted by al-Bukhari and Muslim, concerns Khabbab ibn al-Aratt and al-As ibn Wa'il, who refused to repay a debt unless Khabbab denied Muhammad. Al-Hasan attributes it instead to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and al-Qurtubi judges the first view the sounder. Al-Mawardi, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur also note the debate over whether children will exist in Paradise.

God tells us that the polytheists took deities besides Him, idols and others, so that they would be a source of might and support for them, that is, intercessors who would save them from punishment. God rejects their claim with the word "kalla", meaning: it is not so. The commentators agree that these deities will disown the worship offered to them on the Day of Resurrection, but they differ on who the pronoun in "they will disbelieve" refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi hold that it is the deities who deny the worship of the idolaters, citing the verse: "We disown before You what they used to worship." Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya allow that it may be the idolaters who deny having worshipped them, out of fear of the bad outcome, as in: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."

On the meaning of "didd", the views vary. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean helpers who will oppose them in their disputes, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to mean companions in the Fire who curse one another, al-Dahhak takes it to mean enemies, and Ibn Zayd takes it to mean a trial. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as meaning support, and note that it is singular because the sense is unified. Abu Nuhayk's reading of "kullan" and "kullu" is reported by al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya.

The next verse explains that the devils were sent against the disbelievers to incite them to sin. Al-Razi understands the sending as empowerment over them, while others understand it as merely leaving them free to do so. The commentators emphasise that God does not hasten their punishment, because He counts their deeds and even their breaths.

This verse reports that the idolaters took deities besides God, hoping they would bring them honour, intercession and protection before God. The opening word "kallā" rejects that hope: things are not as they imagine. The commentators broadly agree that these deities will disown their worship on the Day of Resurrection. They differ, however, on who the pronoun refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the worshipped deities, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that it may also refer to the idolaters, who will deny having worshipped them out of fear of the bad outcome. As for the word "didd", al-Tabari explains that in Arabic it means opposition and contrariness. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read it as helpers, Qatada as companions in the Fire who curse one another, al-Dahhak as enemies, and Ibn Zayd as a calamity. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari understand it as the opposite of honour, that is humiliation, and al-Zamakhshari explains the singular form by the unity of their cause. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention the varied readings of "kallā" reported from Abu Nuhayk. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the verse may be a message of good news to the Prophet that his religion will prevail over idolatry.

The commentators explain that the verse means God has set the devils upon the disbelievers, who stir them up, agitate them and urge them toward disobedience until they fall into it. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and most exegetes take the verb "azz" to mean inciting, provoking and driving toward sins. The meaning of "sending" is debated: al-Zajjaj, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as empowering the devils over the unbelievers or assigning them as companions, while al-Zamakhshari, following the Mu'tazilites, reads it as merely leaving them free without preventing them. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir reject this reading, holding that the language and context require the sense of domination. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also report other explanations of the word, such as urging, rousing or kindling. As for the words "do not hasten against them", they mean the Prophet should not wish their destruction too soon, since God counts their days and even their breaths in order to repay them. Some say that this counting refers to their years and terms, others to their deeds, as Qutrub held. The commentators agree that the passage expresses the Prophet's wonder at the obstinacy of the unbelievers, that their agitation results from satanic seduction, and that the verse consoles the Prophet as a conclusion to the preceding passages.

The commentators explain the verse as follows: do not hasten, O Prophet, the punishment of these disbelievers, for God counts their deeds, their days and their breaths, and He will delay them only until a fixed term, neither earlier nor later. Nearly all agree that the verb yaʾuzzuhum means to incite, provoke and drive them towards disobedience and disbelief, as al-Tabari reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, the root meaning being the boiling of a cooking pot. On what is counted in the phrase nuʿiddu lahum ʿaddan, opinions differ: al-Kalbi says the days, nights, months and years, Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil say the breaths, Qutrub says their deeds, and Muqatil says the length of their respite before they are punished. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyya understand that the time between the Prophet and their destruction is short and limited, and al-Razi sees the verse as a consolation for the Prophet. The commentators do not choose between these views, and several cite the anecdote of Ibn al-Sammak before al-Ma'mun on how quickly breaths are spent, along with Ibn ʿAbbas's saying that the last count is the departure of the soul.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will gather the God-fearing before the Most Merciful as a delegation. The commentators agree that wafd means riders: Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Ibn Jurayj and al-Thawri say so, and a report attributed to Ali describes them being brought on camels of Paradise with saddles of gold, as an honour. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir read the image as one of respect, like delegations that come before kings hoping for their favour, so it does not imply departure. Al-Mawardi notes other possible meanings, such as groups or visitors. The sinners, by contrast, will be driven to Hell as a warda, meaning thirsty, according to Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan and Qatada, though some say on foot or alone.

Opinions differ on the statement that they will not possess intercession except for the one who has made a covenant with the Merciful. Ibn Abbas and most exegetes take this covenant to be the testimony that there is no god but Allah, lived out in action. Others see it as the permission to intercede granted by God, a reading Ibn Juzayy considers more likely. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi hold that believing sinners may receive intercession and cite traditions about the Prophet's intercession, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir add reports about scholars and martyrs interceding. Some read the pronoun as referring to the pious and others to the wrongdoers, and the commentators leave these readings side by side without choosing among them.

This verse describes how the wrongdoers will be driven to Hell on the Day of Resurrection, parched with thirst, as cattle are led to water. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan and Qatada explain the word "waradan" as meaning thirsty. Al-Farra', al-Akhfash and Ibn al-A'rabi understand it as on foot, and others say they will come singly. Ibn Kathir and other commentators see no contradiction, since they will be driven on foot, thirsty and scattered. The verb "nasuq", to drive, conveys compulsion and humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also see irony here, since "ward" normally means coming to water, yet it leads to Hell. The word is a verbal noun for going to water, and it is also used for the people who come to it.

Commentators link this verse to the one before it, where the pious are gathered to the Merciful as honoured delegations. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi present the two groups as contrasted. The next verse, "they shall have no power of intercession", divides the scholars. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that only one who has made a covenant with the Merciful, namely the testimony of God's oneness and good deeds, can intercede. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that no one may intercede without the permission of the Merciful. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the covenant might refer to the Prophet's own intercession.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Day of Resurrection: neither the disbelievers nor the beings they took besides God have any intercession that could benefit them. Only one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful possesses intercession, meaning one who has realised faith and righteous deeds. Ibn 'Abbas explains that this covenant is the testimony that there is no god but God, together with disavowing one's own power and strength; Ibn Mas'ud relates a supplication the believer recites morning and evening to form this covenant; Qatada takes it to mean obedience to God, and as-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj say good deeds. Others, citing verses such as 'No intercession avails except for one whom the Most Merciful permits,' understand the covenant as God's permission and command to intercede. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others allow that the pronoun of 'they do not possess' may include all servants, making the exception continuous, whereas others restrict it to the disbelievers and treat the exception as discontinuous. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that scholars, martyrs and the righteous will intercede, relying on hadiths, and some see here the general intercession of the Prophet ﷺ. The commentators agree that this intercession depends on faith rather than on the idols, and that polytheists will find no one to intercede for them, which emphasises the terror of that day.

This verse reports the words of the disbelievers: "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son." The commentators identify the speakers as the Jews who said Uzayr is the son of God, the Christians who said the same of the Messiah, and some Arabs who held that the angels are God's daughters. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain "a monstrous thing" (shay'an idda) as something outrageous and grave, and the word idd conveys severity and enormity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi connect the phrase "from it" to this shocking statement: the heavens almost split, the earth is almost rent and the mountains collapse, so great is the enormity of the words. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read this as a rhetorical image of the statement's damage to the foundations of faith, while Abu Muslim holds that the cosmos would react this way if it could understand.

The commentators agree that the Most Merciful is exalted above having a son and that all beings in the heavens and the earth are His servants, who will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection after He has counted them. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn Sa'di note that begetting a son implies need and deficiency, while al-Alusi and al-Qasimi argue that the name "Most Merciful" implies a mercy embracing all creation, which is incompatible with such filiation. Al-Tha'alibi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the word "love" (wudd) in the next verse to mean the affection God places in the hearts of believers. Accounts of the occasion of revelation, linked to 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf or to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, differ, and the commentators do not settle between them.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses those who claimed that the All-Merciful has taken a son, whether the Arabs who said the angels are God's daughters, or the Jews and Christians. The common meaning is: you have uttered a monstrous and enormous thing. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain the word idd as great or outrageous, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note three readings of the word, all close in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari reads the following verses, in which the heavens nearly split, the earth cracks and the mountains collapse, as an exaggeration meant to convey the gravity of the words: if inanimate things could understand, they would react in this way out of anger for God. Al-Baydawi takes a similar view, presenting it as an image of how terrible the statement is. Ibn Abbas and Ka'b report, as cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, that the heavens, the earth and the mountains were struck with fear, while al-Razi gives other explanations, including that God restrains His punishment out of forbearance. The readers differ on some verb forms without changing the general sense of near-rupture. Several scholars, such as Ibn Ashur, note the shift from the third person to the second, which serves to deliver a direct rebuke. The commentators then affirm that God is exalted above having a child, and that all who are in the heavens and the earth are His servants, coming to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection.

This verse describes how monstrous the claim is that the Merciful has taken a son. The commentators explain that the heavens nearly split apart, the earth nearly cracks open, and the mountains nearly collapse in ruin, all because the statement is so grave and provokes divine anger. They agree that the word idd means something hideous and enormous, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Muqatil report, and that the verse refutes attributing a son to God. Al-Tabari quotes Ibn 'Abbas that the verse expresses the gravity of association, since all creatures except humans and jinn would have been terrified by it. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the splitting, cracking and collapse as ruin or divine wrath. Al-Zamakhshari sees a figure of speech emphasising the enormity of the words and their damage to religion, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as hyperbole meant to alarm. Commentators differ on the meaning of the splitting and cracking: some take it as a fear-induced rupture, others as a collapse falling upon those who uttered the claim. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi note that the verb yakadu may be used figuratively. The recitations vary in the verb forms, but most scholars hold that the meaning remains essentially the same. The commentators conclude that a son is unfitting for God, since all in the heavens and on earth are His servants, He has counted them, and each of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the enormity of the claim that the Most Merciful has taken a son, whether the Arabs said this of the angels, the Jews of Uzayr, or the Christians of the Messiah. The plain meaning is that the saying is so appalling that the heavens almost split apart, the earth is torn open and the mountains collapse. Ibn Abbas and Ka'b report that all creation was struck with fear except the two weighty beings, humans and jinn. Others, such as al-Zamakhshari, read the image as an exaggeration meant to convey the gravity of the words and their damage to religion, rather than as a literal event. All agree that God has no son, since a son implies kinship, origin and resemblance, none of which befit Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi stress that everything in the heavens and on earth is His servant, that He has counted them all, and that each will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection. The readings differ: Nafi and al-Kisai read the verb in the third person masculine, while others read it in the feminine, and some read the word for splitting as yanfatirna, others as yatafattarna. Concerning the word idden, the majority reading with a kasra is joined by variants with a fatha and with an alif. On the grammatical role of the clause beginning with an da'aw, the commentators differ: some take it as a substitute for the pronoun in minhu, some as an object of purpose, and some as the subject of hadden. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take da'aw to mean naming or attributing.

The commentators explain that this verse firmly denies that the Most Merciful could take a son: it does not befit Him, and it is not conceivable for Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that a child implies kinship of nature and need, from which God is free, and that all creatures in the heavens and the earth are His servants who will come to Him humbly on the Day of Resurrection, with no kinship between them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi clarify that the verb yanbaghi means 'what cannot come about': it is an impossibility, not a sign of divine inability. Al-Nasafi notes that the repeated name al-Rahman shows that everything other than God is a blessing or one blessed, so He cannot be compared to a son as the source of all blessings. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur see the verse as a reply to the polytheists who said the angels are God's daughters, and as an indirect rebuke to the Christians who attributed a son to God.

The commentators agree that this verse follows a description of that saying as monstrous: according to Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b, the heavens, the earth and the mountains were terrified by it, and only the two species of humans and jinn were not. Ibn Kathir sees in this a glorification of God. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report the variant readings of 'atin' and 'wuldan' without any change in meaning. Al-Qurtubi draws from the verse that a child cannot be owned by his father, since filiation and servitude are opposites.

Al-Sha'rawi distinguishes between the thing being impossible and its being unfitting: God could have had a son, but it does not befit Him.

The commentators explain that this verse states that everyone in the heavens and on earth, angels, humans and jinn alike, will come to the Most Merciful on the Day of Resurrection as a humble and submissive servant. Since sonship and servitude cannot coexist, none of them can be a son of God. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari read it as a rebuttal of those who ascribe a child to God, and it follows verses describing the terror that the creation feels at such a claim. Al-Tabari understands the coming as submission and acknowledgement, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi describe it as taking refuge in God through servitude and obedience. Al-Alusi also mentions the possibility of a literal coming to the place of gathering.

The commentators agree that the verse denies any divine filiation, that all creatures are His servants, and that His knowledge encompasses them. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi add that each will come alone that day, with neither wealth nor helper. Al-Qurtubi reports that some jurists drew from the verse the ruling that a father who comes to own his child frees him, and that Ibn Rahawayh applied a similar reasoning to slave women, a point on which al-Qurtubi notes differing opinions.

Ibn 'Atiyya links the verse to what precedes it: after describing everyone's coming in servitude and isolation, God reassures the believers by promising that He will give them affection, meaning signs of His favour, on that day. He notes that most exegetes take this affection to be the acceptance God places in the hearts of those He loves, in line with a hadith transmitted from Abu Hurayra.

This verse says that God has encompassed all creatures with His knowledge and counted them precisely, so that none of them is hidden from Him and their number is not lost on Him. The commentators read it as a response to those who claimed that the Merciful has a son, since the whole creation is subject to Him and numbered by Him. Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi explain ihsa' as restriction and encompassing by knowledge, and 'add as reinforcing and confirming that meaning. Ibn Kathir specifies that it refers to the counting of every being from its creation until the Day of Resurrection, while al-Mawardi, citing Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, says the counting covers their breaths, their days and their traces. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand that God counts persons, their breaths and their deeds, and that nothing small or great escapes Him. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the repetition of the meaning in different words to be emphasis. The Jalalayn summarise it as meaning that the total of them, and not a single one, is hidden from God. Al-Alusi gives the same sense. The commentators agree that the verse brings comfort to believers and warning to those who deny. It contains no legal ruling, and the exegetes report no particular occasion of revelation for this passage.

The commentators explain that this verse comes in response to those who claimed God has a son, whether Jews and Christians or Arab polytheists who said the angels are God's daughters. God states that He has counted His creation exactly, that nothing escapes Him, and that each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, stripped of wealth, children, and helpers. Ibn 'Abbas and others add that all beings are His obedient servants, so none of them can be His offspring.

The scholars agree on the core message: the verse rules out any divine offspring or partner and affirms God's complete knowledge. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read the word "fardan" as being alone without wealth or supporters. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi understand it more as being separated from followers and allies, so that neither the worshipped nor the worshippers keep any tie. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that the singular "ātīhi" expresses each person's separation even when they all arrive together, and he prefers this reading to the grammatical explanation based on the construction of "kull".

Al-Zamakhshari notes that "kulluhum" may take either a singular or plural verb, and Ibn 'Ashur points out that the repeated name "al-Rahman" shows that such a filiation contradicts divine mercy. Al-Qurtubi draws a legal point: a son cannot be owned as a slave by his father, since sonship and servitude are opposite states. Most other commentaries focus on the general meaning of the verse and its place within the surah.

The commentators explain that this verse promises believers who do righteous deeds that the Most Merciful will place affection for them in the hearts of people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand wudd as love set in the hearts of the believers, and they report from Mujahid and Ibn Abbas that God loves them and makes them beloved to His servants. The commentators agree that this love is not earned through kinship or self-interest but is a gift from God, and they cite the hadith narrated by Abu Hurayra about Gabriel being called and then acceptance being placed on earth. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the sin in sayaj'alu may indicate a promise made during the Meccan period or a fulfilment on the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim, as quoted by al-Razi, takes wudd to mean what is loved, that is, what God will give them in Paradise, but al-Razi and most scholars prefer the first meaning.

They differ on when this is fulfilled: most say it happens in this world, while some, such as al-Jubba'i, place it in the Hereafter, when good deeds are displayed and rancour is removed from hearts. As for the occasion of revelation, al-Tabari reports it concerned Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, but Ibn Kathir considers this an error since the surah is Meccan; others name Ali ibn Abi Talib, and some refrain from deciding. The word luddan is explained as fierce adversaries in dispute, generally identified with the Quraysh. The commentators conclude that the Quran was made easy in the Prophet's tongue to bring good news to the pious and warn the stubborn, and that the verse ends by recalling the destruction of earlier generations.

The commentators explain that God made the Qur'an easy by revealing it in the clear Arabic tongue of the Prophet ﷺ, so that he might give good news to the God-conscious and warn a stubbornly hostile people. Nearly all of them identify this people with the Quraysh of Mecca. The meaning of 'ludd', the plural of 'alad', varies: Mujahid takes it as wicked sinners, Ibn 'Abbas as wrongdoers, al-Hasan as deaf to the truth, Qatada as people who argue falsely, and Abu 'Ubayda as those who reject truth and claim falsehood. The majority combines these into the sense of fierce, obstinate quarrelsomeness. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that this word answers the mention of the God-conscious, since one who clings to falsehood and argues for it is furthest from piety. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the word 'people' shows that this contentiousness is their defining trait, and that their disbelief stemmed from willful opposition despite knowing the truth. The verse closes the surah and leads into the mention of earlier generations destroyed, of whom no trace or sound remains. The particle 'fa' introduces a conclusion drawn from the context: conveying the message, giving good tidings and warning. The commentators agree that the Qur'an is made easy to understand and to memorize in the Arabic language.

At the close of Surah Maryam, God addresses His Prophet ﷺ and warns the Quraysh by pointing to the fate of the earlier peoples. He destroyed many generations before them for rejecting their messengers, so that no trace of them can be seen and no faint sound of them can be heard. The commentators explain rikz as a faint sound, following Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak, or as anything barely perceptible, following al-Yazidi and Abu Ubayda, who cite a verse of Labid. Ibn Zayd takes it to mean any perception at all. They agree that the question is rhetorical and negative, meant to frighten the opponents and to console the Prophet.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that the destruction was so complete that nothing remains of those peoples, and that the Meccans face the same end unless they repent. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the destruction may mean death or an immediate punishment in this world, though al-Razi considers the disappearance through death the more likely meaning. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur explain that qarn means a nation or a generation, and that kam expresses a great number.

The verse follows the statement that God made the Quran easy in the Prophet's tongue, to give good news to the righteous and to warn a stubborn people, the luddun. Most commentators identify them as the Quraysh, though Ibn Abbas understands them as sinners, Hasan as the deaf to truth and Ibn Kathir as those who turn aside from what is right.
